one: The internet's phone book: turns a name like api.example.com into an IP address a computer can connect to.
an: You know your friend's name, not their phone number. DNS is the contacts app that looks the number up, and it remembers recent answers so it does not have to ask every time.
how: Your browser asks a resolver (usually your ISP's, or 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8). If the resolver has no cached answer it walks the tree: root servers → the .com servers → the domain's own authoritative nameserver, which holds the real records.
Common records: A (name → IPv4), AAAA (→ IPv6), CNAME (alias to another name), MX (mail), TXT (verification, SPF), NS (who is authoritative).
Every answer has a TTL (time to live, in seconds). Resolvers cache it for that long. That is why DNS changes "take time to propagate": old answers live in caches until their TTL runs out.
why: Servers change IPs; names stay stable. DNS also lets one name point to many IPs (basic load spreading) or to a CDN edge near the user.
trade: Lower the TTL a day before a migration so the switch is fast; keep it high normally to reduce lookups. A CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex (example.com itself), which is why providers invent ALIAS/ANAME records.

myth.m: I changed the DNS record, so everyone sees the new server now.
myth.r: Everyone sees it after their cached copy expires. With a TTL of 86400 that can be a full day.

q.s: You will move your API to a new server on Friday. The A record has TTL 86400. What should you do on Wednesday?
o: Nothing, DNS updates instantly
Lower the TTL to something like 300 so caches refresh quickly at cutover
Delete the record so nobody caches it
Switch it to a CNAME
q.e: Caches keep the old answer for up to the TTL. Lower it ahead of time, wait out the old TTL, then switch. Deleting the record causes an outage.

lab: Run dig example.com and read the ANSWER section: record type, TTL, IP.
Run dig +trace example.com and follow the walk from the root servers to the authoritative nameserver.
Run dig example.com twice against 1.1.1.1 (dig @1.1.1.1 ...) and watch the TTL count down between runs: that is the cache.
Look up a CNAME chain: dig www.github.com. Note which names are aliases.
For a domain you own, find its NS records and its TTLs, and write down what you would change before migrating it.

plain:
Computers find each other by number (IP address), but people use names. DNS is the system that turns a name like api.example.com into a number like 104.21.3.7.

Answers are cached for a time you choose (the TTL). That is why a DNS change is not instant: everyone keeps using their saved answer until it expires.
bridge: When you connect a domain to Netlify or Vercel, you add a DNS record (A or CNAME) at your domain provider. When a newly connected domain “doesn't work yet”, it is usually DNS caching.

walk.title: What happens when you open shop.example.com for the first time
steps: Your browser (through a small “stub resolver” in the operating system) asks a recursive resolver, for example your ISP's or 1.1.1.1: “What is the IP for shop.example.com?” It has no saved answer.
The resolver asks a root server: “Who handles .com?” It gets the .com servers.
It asks the .com servers: “Who handles example.com?” It gets example.com's own nameservers (for example, Cloudflare's).
It asks those: “What is shop.example.com?” Answer: CNAME shop.netlify.app with TTL 3600. The resolver now looks up shop.netlify.app the same way and gets an IP.
The browser connects to that IP. For the next hour (3600 s), everyone using that resolver gets the saved answer instantly.

terms: The numeric address of a machine on the internet.
How many seconds an answer may be cached.
The server that holds the real records for a domain.
insights: “It works for me but not for my colleague” after a DNS change is almost always caching: you and your colleague use different resolvers with different cached copies.
Whoever can edit your DNS records can point your domain anywhere and even get a valid HTTPS certificate for it. Treat DNS access like production database access.
Every new connection starts with a lookup. In most apps it is cached and cheap, but in Kubernetes or in processes that never re-resolve, DNS quietly becomes a latency or correctness problem.

prod.summary: In production, DNS is a dependency you rarely think about until a migration, a certificate check or a Kubernetes cluster makes it slow or wrong. Seniors care about three things: who controls the zone (and how it is protected), what the TTLs are before any change, and how many lookups the app really does per request.
checklist: Registrar and DNS provider accounts have 2FA, and at least two people can log in. Losing the domain means losing the whole product.
Before a migration: lower the TTL to 60–300 s, then wait at least the old TTL before you switch the record.
Check the change at the source first: dig @<authoritative-ns> name. If the authoritative server is right, the rest is only caching.
Use ALIAS/ANAME or the provider's flattening for the zone apex (example.com), never a CNAME there.
Mail records (MX, SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT) are moved together with the zone, or email silently breaks.
In Kubernetes, look at ndots in the pod's /etc/resolv.conf; call external hosts with a trailing dot or lower ndots to cut wasted lookups.
Long-running clients (Node services, JVM, connection pools) must re-resolve names; a process that cached an IP at startup will keep using the old server after a move.
numbers: Cloudflare proxied records always have TTL “Auto” = 300 s; DNS-only records can go down to 60 s (30 s on Enterprise).
Kubernetes pods get ndots:5 by default, so a name with fewer than 5 dots is first tried against every search domain (several extra queries per lookup).
DNS Flag Day 2020 recommends an EDNS UDP buffer of 1232 bytes; larger answers are truncated and retried over TCP port 53.
Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too, for the SOA record's negative TTL (RFC 2308).
failures: After a server move, some users still hit the old IP a day later.

The old record had TTL 86400 and was not lowered in advance, or a long-running process cached the IP. Lower TTLs before migrations, keep the old server serving (or redirecting) until the old TTL has passed, and restart or re-resolve in long-lived clients.
A new subdomain shows NXDOMAIN for some people for an hour after you created it.

Someone (or a health check) looked it up before it existed, and the resolver cached the negative answer for the SOA negative TTL. Create records before you announce them, and check the SOA minimum TTL.
p99 latency of outbound calls from Kubernetes pods is high; CoreDNS CPU is busy.

ndots:5 makes api.stripe.com go through the search list first (api.stripe.com.default.svc.cluster.local, ...), each one a miss. Use fully qualified names with a trailing dot, set dnsConfig.options ndots: 2, or run NodeLocal DNSCache.
Let's Encrypt or email verification suddenly fails with a DNS error.
A stale CAA record forbids the CA, or a dangling CNAME points to a deleted cloud resource. Audit the zone; dangling CNAMEs are also a subdomain-takeover risk.

code.title: Checking a DNS change at the source before blaming caches
code.src:
# 1. Who is authoritative for the zone?
dig +short NS example.com

# 2. Ask the authoritative server directly: this is the truth, no cache
dig +noall +answer @ns1.example-dns.com api.example.com A

# 3. Ask public resolvers: the TTL column counts down from the cached copy
dig +noall +answer @1.1.1.1 api.example.com A
dig +noall +answer @8.8.8.8 api.example.com A

# 4. Before a migration: confirm the lowered TTL is really live (prints the TTL)
dig +noall +answer @ns1.example-dns.com api.example.com A | awk '{print $2}'
code.note: If step 2 shows the new IP and step 3 the old one, your change is correct and you are only waiting for caches. The TTL in step 3 tells you how long. Put +noall +answer before @server: older dig builds (macOS ships 9.10) otherwise still print header lines, and step 4 would feed them to awk.

qs.s: Your app's own domain is shop.com. Marketing wants shop.com (no www) to point to a Netlify site whose target is shop.netlify.app. Your DNS provider rejects a CNAME on shop.com. What is the right fix?
o: Put an A record pointing to the IP you get when you ping shop.netlify.app
Use a CNAME on shop.com anyway through the API
Use the provider's ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME flattening, or the host's documented apex A record
Lower the TTL so the CNAME is accepted
qs.e: A CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex because the apex must also hold SOA and NS records. ALIAS/flattening resolves the target for you and returns A records. Copying an IP you pinged looks like it works but breaks when the platform changes that IP.

qs.s: At 10:00 you change an A record. The old record had TTL 3600. A resolver fetched it at 09:55. At 10:20 a user behind that resolver still gets the old IP. When will that resolver, at the latest, return the new IP?
o: About 10:55
About 10:20, it should already be updated
About 11:00
Never, until the resolver is restarted
qs.e: The resolver may keep the cached answer for the full TTL from when it fetched it: 09:55 + 3600 s = 10:55. The time you changed the record does not matter for already-cached copies.

qs.s: A Node service running for weeks keeps calling the old IP of a partner API that moved last night. Other services and dig show the new IP. What is the most likely cause?
o: The partner's TTL is too low
The DNS provider did not propagate the change
HTTP/2 is caching DNS
The process (or its connection pool) holds open connections or a cached IP from before the move and never re-resolves
qs.e: dig already returns the new IP, so DNS itself is correct. Long-lived keep-alive connections and app-level DNS caches keep talking to the old address. Cap connection lifetime and let the client re-resolve.

qs.s: You plan to move www.shop.com from CDN A to CDN B by changing the CNAME target. A resolver fetched this answer one second ago. In the worst case, how long will that resolver keep sending users to CDN A?

code.title: dig www.shop.com
code.src:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
www.shop.com.            3600  IN  CNAME  shop.cdn-a.net.
shop.cdn-a.net.            20  IN  A      203.0.113.7

o: About 20 seconds, the shortest TTL in the chain
About 1 hour and 20 seconds, the TTLs add up
About 1 hour, because the CNAME record itself is cached for 3600 s
No time, a CNAME change is applied instantly
qs.e: Each record in the chain is cached on its own, with its own TTL. You are changing the CNAME record, and that record may be cached for 3600 s. The 20 s TTL only controls how fast CDN A can change its own IPs. Lower the TTL of your record before the move.

qs.s: A pod in Kubernetes calls api.stripe.com. All search domains return NXDOMAIN. How many wrong names does the resolver try (per record type) before it asks for api.stripe.com. itself?

code.title: /etc/resolv.conf inside the pod
code.src:
nameserver 10.96.0.10
search payments.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local eu-west-1.compute.internal
options ndots:5

o: 0, because api.stripe.com already has a dot
1, only the first search domain
5, one per dot plus one
4, one for each search domain
qs.e: The name has 2 dots, fewer than ndots:5, so the resolver treats it as “maybe local” and tries every search domain first: 4 misses, then the real name. With A and AAAA queried, that is 8 wasted queries per lookup. A trailing dot (api.stripe.com.) or ndots: 2 skips them.

qs.s: Your zone still has docs.example.com CNAME example-docs.herokuapp.com, but the Heroku app was deleted last year. What is the real risk?
o: Someone else can create an app with that Heroku name and serve their content on docs.example.com (subdomain takeover)
None, the name just returns an error
Heroku will bill you for the old app
Email to example.com stops working
qs.e: A dangling CNAME points to a name you no longer own. If the platform lets anyone claim that name, an attacker serves pages, phishing forms or cookie-stealing scripts on your trusted subdomain. Delete records together with the resources they point to, and scan the zone for dangling CNAMEs.

qs.s: You use DNS-based failover with TTL 60 s: when region A fails, the record switches to region B. In a real incident, about 10% of traffic still reaches the dead region 15 minutes later. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Some resolvers and clients keep answers longer than the TTL (minimum-TTL clamping, JVM or app-level DNS caches, long-lived keep-alive connections)
The authoritative nameserver did not update
TTL 60 s is too short and the resolvers rejected it
Region B's firewall blocked the traffic
qs.e: TTL is a maximum the resolver should respect, not a guarantee. Some resolvers raise very low TTLs, some runtimes cache DNS themselves, and open connections never re-resolve at all. DNS failover is useful but slow and partial; for fast failover put an anycast or global load balancer in front, which changes routing without waiting for caches.

interview.q: Walk me through the DNS part of opening https://example.com for the first time. Where can it be slow or fail?
answer: The browser and OS check their own caches, then ask the configured recursive resolver (ISP, 1.1.1.1, or the corporate/Kubernetes resolver).
On a cache miss the resolver walks root → .com TLD → the domain's authoritative nameservers, following CNAMEs, and caches every answer for its TTL (negative answers too, via the SOA).
Slow points: a cold cache (several round trips), a far or overloaded resolver, search-domain expansion (ndots in Kubernetes), and large answers that fall back from UDP to TCP.
Failure points: wrong delegation (NS at the registrar does not match the provider), expired domain, DNSSEC signature errors (SERVFAIL), cached NXDOMAIN, dangling CNAMEs.
Debug from the source outward: dig @authoritative first, then public resolvers, then the client's own resolver.
followups: Why can a CNAME not sit at the zone apex?
What does a resolver return when DNSSEC validation fails?

interview.q: How would you move a production domain from one DNS provider to another with zero downtime?
answer: Export the full zone and recreate every record at the new provider, including MX, SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT, CAA and verification records, not only A/CNAME.
Verify the new zone before switching: dig @new-ns for every important name must match dig @old-ns.
Lower record TTLs ahead of time. The NS delegation TTL at the parent (often 1–2 days) is set by the TLD, not by you, so keep both providers serving identical zones for at least that long.
If DNSSEC is on, plan it explicitly: either a multi-signer setup or remove the DS record, wait out its TTL, migrate, then re-sign. A wrong DS record makes the whole domain fail with SERVFAIL.
Freeze record changes during the window, or apply every change at both providers.
followups: What breaks first if you forget the MX records?
How do you prove resolvers worldwide see the new nameservers?

interview.q: Outbound calls from our Kubernetes services have high p99 latency, and CoreDNS CPU is high. How do you investigate and fix it?
answer: Check the pod's /etc/resolv.conf: ndots:5 plus several search domains turns one external lookup into many queries (A and AAAA for each).
Look at CoreDNS metrics: request rate per type, NXDOMAIN ratio, cache hit ratio. A high NXDOMAIN ratio confirms search-path waste.
Fixes: use fully qualified names with a trailing dot, set dnsConfig.options ndots: 2 for pods that mostly call external hosts, enable NodeLocal DNSCache, scale CoreDNS.
Check the app side too: clients that resolve on every request (no connection reuse) multiply DNS load; a keep-alive pool reduces it.
Watch for the conntrack race on UDP DNS (parallel A/AAAA), which shows as 5 s timeouts; NodeLocal DNSCache or single-request-reopen helps.
followups: Why do 5-second delays point to DNS timeouts?
What is the trade-off of caching DNS inside the application?

diagrams.title: First lookup of shop.example.com, then the cache
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant R as Resolver (ISP or 1.1.1.1)
  participant Root as Root server
  participant TLD as .com servers
  participant NS as example.com nameserver
  B->>R: IP for shop.example.com?
  Note over R: no cached answer
  R->>Root: who handles .com?
  Root-->>R: ask the .com servers
  R->>TLD: who handles example.com?

one: Two ways of sending data over IP. TCP is a reliable, ordered conversation; UDP is fire-and-forget packets.
an: TCP is a phone call: you connect, every sentence arrives in order, and you notice if the line drops. UDP is shouting across a room: fast, but nobody guarantees the other person heard every word.
how: IP delivers packets between machines but promises nothing about order or delivery. TCP and UDP sit on top and add ports so many programs can share one IP.

TCP opens with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every byte, re-sends lost packets, and slows down when the network is congested. That costs at least one round trip before any data flows.
UDP just sends datagrams. No handshake, no retries, no ordering. The application deals with loss, or accepts it.
why: Most of the web (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, databases, SSH) needs every byte intact, so it uses TCP. Video calls, games and DNS prefer UDP because a late packet is worse than a lost one. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which is built on UDP to avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking.
trade: Every new TCP connection costs a round trip (plus more for TLS). This is the reason connection reuse, keep-alive and connection pools matter so much.

myth.m: UDP is unreliable, so it is bad.
myth.r: UDP is minimal. Protocols like QUIC build their own reliability on top of it, tuned better than TCP for the job.

q.s: Your service opens a brand-new database connection for each request, and p50 latency is mostly connection setup. What is the underlying cost you are paying?
o: UDP packet loss
A TCP handshake (and usually TLS + auth) on every request
DNS propagation
HTTP caching misses
q.e: Each new TCP connection needs a handshake round trip, then TLS and DB auth. A connection pool reuses open connections so you pay it once.

plain:
Data travels the internet in small packets. Packets can get lost, duplicated or arrive in the wrong order. TCP fixes all of that: it makes a connection, numbers every piece, and resends anything lost. UDP does not: it just sends packets and hopes.

TCP is reliable but needs a short “hello” exchange before sending data, and that costs time on every new connection.
bridge: In DevTools → Network → Timing, the “Initial connection” and “SSL” bars are the TCP and TLS setup. They appear only on the first request to a server; later requests reuse the connection and skip them.

walk.title: Why the first request to a far server is slow
steps: Your user in Tashkent requests your API in the US. One round trip (there and back) takes about 200ms.
TCP handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. One round trip: 200ms before any data.
TLS handshake for HTTPS: about one more round trip: 400ms total.
Now the actual request and response: another round trip: about 600ms total for a tiny response.
The second request on the same connection needs only the last round trip: about 200ms. Connection reuse and servers close to users matter a lot.

terms: A small chunk of data sent over the network.
The setup messages exchanged before real data flows.
Time for a message to go there and back.
A number that says which program on the machine should receive the data.
insights: Latency (distance) often matters more than bandwidth for web apps. Fewer round trips beat a faster connection.

TCP only promises that bytes reached the other machine's network stack, not that the app handled them. If the connection dies after you send a request, you do not know whether it ran, so you still need idempotency and retries at the application level.
Video calls and games use UDP because a late packet is useless; they prefer dropping it to waiting.

prod.summary: In production, TCP shows up as latency (handshakes on every new connection), as resource limits (ephemeral ports, TIME_WAIT, file descriptors) and as timeouts that disagree between layers. Seniors make sure connections are reused, timeouts are set on purpose, and they know when a UDP-based protocol (DNS, QUIC, WebRTC) will be blocked by a firewall.
checklist: Outbound HTTP and database calls reuse connections (keep-alive agent or pool). A new TCP + TLS connection per request is a review blocker.
Every outbound call has a connect timeout and a total timeout. Without them a dead peer can hang a request for minutes.
Idle timeouts are ordered: client < load balancer < server keep-alive, so the side that closes first is the one that does not send.
Dashboards show connection counts and TIME_WAIT sockets (ss -s), not only request rate.
The process ulimit -n (open files) is high enough for the expected sockets; each connection is one file descriptor.
For UDP-based features (QUIC, WebRTC, DNS), there is a TCP fallback, because many corporate networks block UDP.
numbers: Linux default ephemeral port range is 32768–60999 (about 28,000 ports) per source IP / destination IP+port pair.
Linux keeps a closed connection in TIME_WAIT for 60 s on the side that closed first.
The initial congestion window is 10 segments (RFC 6928), about 14 KB, so the first round trip of a new connection can deliver only about 14 KB.
Linux tcp_syn_retries defaults to 6, which means a connect to a silent host can wait about 2 minutes unless the app sets its own connect timeout.
failures: Under load, outbound calls fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL or connect EADDRINUSE; ss -s shows tens of thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT.
The service opens a new connection for each request and closes it, so ports pile up in TIME_WAIT for 60 s. Use a keep-alive agent / pool so connections are reused.
Requests to another service hang for about 2 minutes, then fail with ETIMEDOUT.
The target host is gone and packets are dropped silently, so the OS keeps retrying SYN. Set an explicit connect timeout (1–3 s) and a total timeout on every client.
Random ECONNRESET / socket hang up on the first request after a quiet period.

The server or a middlebox closed the idle keep-alive connection, and the client reused it at the same moment. Make the client's idle timeout shorter than the server's, and retry idempotent requests once.
Video calls or an HTTP/3 rollout work at home but not in some offices.
The office firewall blocks UDP. Browsers fall back from HTTP/3 to HTTP/2 over TCP automatically; WebRTC needs a TURN server on TCP/TLS 443 as a fallback.

code.title: Reusing outbound connections from Node with explicit timeouts
code.note: keepAliveTimeout applies when the server sends no Keep-Alive: timeout=N hint; keep it below the server's idle timeout (Node's default is 5 s), so the client drops an idle socket before the server closes it under the client's feet. When the server does send the hint, undici uses N minus 2 s instead.

qs.s: A user is 150 ms RTT away. A cold HTTPS request with TLS 1.3 needs: TCP handshake, TLS handshake, then request/response. Roughly how long until the first byte arrives, ignoring server time?
o: 150 ms
300 ms
600 ms
450 ms
qs.e: One RTT for TCP, one for TLS 1.3, one for the request and response: 3 × 150 = 450 ms. A reused connection needs only the last RTT. TLS 1.2 would add one more RTT.

qs.s: Your worker sends 2,000 requests per second to one internal API, each on a new connection that it closes. After a few minutes calls fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL. Which change fixes the root cause?
o: Raise the API's CPU limit
Reuse connections with a keep-alive agent or pool
Switch the API to UDP
Increase the DNS TTL
qs.e: 2,000 closes/s × 60 s TIME_WAIT = 120,000 sockets, far more than the ~28,000 ephemeral ports. Reusing connections removes the churn. Tuning kernel settings only moves the limit.

qs.s: Your team wants to send live game positions 30 times per second. A teammate suggests TCP “because it is reliable”. Why do many games use UDP for this instead?
o: A lost position packet is replaced by the next one 33 ms later, and TCP would block newer data while it resends the old one
UDP is encrypted by default
TCP cannot send more than 10 messages per second
UDP packets always arrive in order
qs.e: With TCP, one lost packet holds back everything after it (head-of-line blocking) until it is resent. For state that is replaced every frame, old data is useless, so dropping it is better. UDP has no built-in encryption or ordering.

qs.s: A worker that calls one internal API shows this on the host. What is the most likely cause?

code.title: ss -s
code.src:
Total: 31250
TCP:   30412 (estab 180, closed 30120, orphaned 0, timewait 30098)

Transport Total     IP        IPv6
TCP       30412     30401     11

o: A SYN flood attack against the worker
A memory leak in the worker process
Connection churn: the worker opens and closes a new connection per call, and closed sockets wait in TIME_WAIT for 60 s
UDP packet loss on the network
qs.e: Only 180 connections are established, but 30,098 are in TIME_WAIT. That is the footprint of many short-lived connections closed by this side. It is close to the ~28,000 ephemeral ports per destination, so EADDRNOTAVAIL is next. Reuse connections with a keep-alive agent or pool. A SYN flood would show many half-open (SYN-RECV) sockets on a server, not TIME_WAIT on a client.

qs.s: Read this TCP server. It works in local tests. In production it sometimes throws SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input or Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON. Why?

code.title: server.ts

o: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries: one data event can hold half a message or two messages
TCP corrupts bytes on slow networks
chunk.toString() uses the wrong encoding
The client must use UDP for JSON
qs.e: TCP guarantees the bytes arrive in order, not that each write() arrives as one data event. On a real network messages get split or merged. Add framing: newline-delimited JSON or a length prefix, and buffer until a full message is there. TCP checksums and retransmits, so bytes are not corrupted.

qs.s: A backup job copies data between two data centres with RTT 100 ms. A middlebox strips TCP window scaling, so the receive window is stuck at 64 KB. The link is 1 Gbit/s. About what throughput will one connection reach?
o: About 1 Gbit/s, the link speed
About 64 KB/s
About 6.4 MB/s
About 640 KB/s (roughly 5 Mbit/s)
qs.e: A sender can have at most one window of unacknowledged data in flight per round trip: 64 KB / 0.1 s = 640 KB/s. The link speed does not matter when the window is the limit. This is the bandwidth-delay product: to fill 1 Gbit/s at 100 ms you need about 12.5 MB in flight.

qs.s: A custom binary protocol over a raw Node net socket writes a 20-byte header and then the body as two separate socket.write() calls. On Linux, each request has about 40 ms of extra latency. What fixes it?

code.title: client.ts

o: Switch to UDP so packets are sent at once
Write header and body in one call (Buffer.concat) and/or call socket.setNoDelay(true)
Increase the socket's receive buffer
Lower the DNS TTL of store.internal
qs.e: Nagle's algorithm holds back a small second write until the first is acknowledged, and the peer's delayed ACK can wait about 40 ms. One combined write, or setNoDelay(true) (TCP_NODELAY), removes the stall. A bigger receive buffer does not change when the sender sends.

interview.q: Why is the first request to a distant server so much slower than the next ones, and what would you do about it?
answer: A cold HTTPS request pays DNS, the TCP handshake (1 RTT), the TLS handshake (1 RTT on TLS 1.3, 2 on TLS 1.2), then the request itself (1 RTT). At 150 ms RTT that is 450 ms before the first byte, without server time.
TCP slow start: the initial congestion window is 10 segments (~14 KB), so a large response needs several more round trips on a new connection.
Reuse connections: keep-alive pools for server-to-server calls, one HTTP/2 connection per origin in browsers, no domain sharding.
Cut RTT: CDN or edge termination near users (TLS ends close to them), regional deployments for APIs.
Cut handshakes: TLS 1.3, session resumption, HTTP/3 (QUIC merges transport and TLS setup), preconnect hints for critical third-party origins.
followups: What does 0-RTT save and what does it risk?
How would you measure each phase from a client?

interview.q: When would you choose UDP over TCP, and what do you have to build yourself if you do?
answer: UDP fits when late data is worthless (voice, video, game state), when you want your own congestion and loss handling (QUIC), or for small request/response protocols (DNS).
You must build or accept: loss detection and retransmission (only where needed), ordering, congestion control (or you hurt the network and yourself), flow control.
Message size: keep datagrams under the path MTU (about 1200 bytes is a safe payload), or handle fragmentation.
Security: no built-in encryption; use DTLS or QUIC. Watch amplification: never send large replies to unverified source addresses.
Operations: many firewalls and corporate networks block UDP, so plan a TCP/TLS 443 fallback (TURN for WebRTC, HTTP/2 for HTTP/3).
followups: Why did HTTP/3 build on UDP instead of fixing TCP?
What is head-of-line blocking at the TCP level?

interview.q: A service sees intermittent ECONNRESET when calling a downstream service. How do you investigate?
answer: Find the pattern: does it happen on the first request after idle time? That points to keep-alive races (the server or a middlebox closed an idle socket just as the client reused it).
Line up idle timeouts: client pool idle < load balancer idle < server keep-alive. Check NAT gateways and firewalls too; some drop idle flows after a few minutes without telling either side.
Check the downstream: crashes, OOM kills or deploys reset open connections; correlate resets with its restarts.
Capture evidence: tcpdump to see who sent the RST, connection metrics, and the client library's retry logs.
Mitigate: retry idempotent requests once on a fresh connection, shorter client idle timeout, graceful shutdown on the server.
followups: Why is retrying a POST after ECONNRESET dangerous?
What is the difference between a RST and a FIN?

diagrams.title: First request to a far server: Tashkent to the US (RTT 200 ms)
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Browser (Tashkent)
  participant S as API server (US)
  C->>S: SYN
  S-->>C: SYN-ACK
  C->>S: ACK
  Note over C,S: TCP ready after 1 RTT (200 ms)
  C->>S: TLS ClientHello
  S-->>C: ServerHello, certificate, Finished
  Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 ready after 2 RTT (400 ms)
  C->>S: GET /api/user
  S-->>C: 200 OK
  Note over C,S: first response after 3 RTT (600 ms)
  C->>S: GET /api/orders (same connection)
  S-->>C: 200 OK
  Note over C,S: reused connection: 1 RTT (200 ms)
diagrams.caption: What to notice: two of the three round trips are setup. Reusing the connection skips them, which is why keep-alive and connection pools matter.

diagrams.title: One lost packet: TCP waits, UDP moves on
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Sender
  participant R as Receiver
  Note over S,R: TCP
  S->>R: segment 1
  S-xR: segment 2 (lost)
  S->>R: segment 3
  R-->>S: ACK, still missing 2
  Note over R: holds 3, app waits
  S->>R: segment 2 (resent)
  Note over R: app gets 1, 2, 3 in order
  Note over S,R: UDP
  S->>R: datagram 1
  S-xR: datagram 2 (lost)
  S->>R: datagram 3
  Note over R: app gets 1 and 3 now, 2 is gone
diagrams.caption: What to notice: TCP delivers everything in order, so one loss delays the bytes behind it (head-of-line blocking). UDP delivers what arrived and leaves loss to the application.

one: The request/response text protocol of the web: a method, a path, headers, an optional body; back comes a status code, headers and a body.
an: A restaurant order slip. The method says what you want done (GET = bring me, POST = make this new thing), the headers are notes for the kitchen, and the status code is the waiter's reply.
how: Methods carry meaning: GET reads, POST creates or triggers, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating them leaves the same result. POST is not.

Status families: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client did something wrong (400 bad input, 401 not authenticated, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 429 too many requests), 5xx the server failed (500, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout).
HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone. Sessions are faked on top with cookies or tokens.
why: Every API you build or call is HTTP. Choosing the right method and status code is how clients, caches, proxies and retries know how to behave without reading your docs.
trade: Returning 200 with {error: ...} in the body breaks every tool that reads status codes: retries, monitoring, caches, alerting.

myth.r: 401 = we do not know who you are (log in). 403 = we know who you are and you are not allowed.

q.s: A gateway in front of your app returns 504. Where should you look first?
o: The client sent bad JSON
The upstream app took too long to answer the gateway
The user is not logged in
DNS is wrong
q.e: 504 Gateway Timeout means the proxy/gateway waited for the upstream server and gave up. 502 means it got an invalid answer, often because the upstream crashed or refused.

more: Safe vs idempotent methods, and why browsers and proxies may retry safe ones
Content negotiation (Accept, Content-Type), compression (gzip, brotli)
Conditional requests (If-None-Match, If-Match for optimistic concurrency)
Redirects: 301/302 vs 307/308 and what happens to the method and body
Problem Details (RFC 9457) as a standard error body format
lab: Make requests with curl -i (show headers) to a public API and read every response header. Look up any you do not know on MDN.
Build a tiny endpoint that returns 201 with a Location header on create, 404 for missing items, 409 on a duplicate, and 422 for validation errors.
Compare curl -I (HEAD) with GET on the same URL.
Trigger a redirect with curl -i http://github.com, then follow it with -L.

plain:
HTTP is the language browsers and servers speak. The client sends a request: a method (what to do), a path (on what), headers (extra info) and maybe a body (data). The server answers with a status code (how it went), headers, and a body.

Each request stands alone; the server does not remember the previous one unless you send something (a cookie or token) that reminds it.
bridge: Every fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers, body }) you write is an HTTP request. res.ok is just “status between 200 and 299”.

walk.title: One HTTP conversation, line by line
steps: Browser sends: POST /api/orders with headers Content-Type: application/json, Cookie: session=abc, and body {"productId": 7}.
Server reads the cookie to know who you are, validates the body, creates the order.
Server answers 201 Created with header Location: /api/orders/512 and the new order as JSON.
If the product did not exist, it would answer 404. If the body was invalid, 422 or 400. If the server crashed, 500.
Your frontend decides what to show based on the status code, not by guessing from the body.

terms: GET (read), POST (create/do), PUT (replace), PATCH (change part), DELETE (remove).
2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx your mistake, 5xx server's mistake.
A key-value note on a request or response, like Content-Type.
Each request is independent; the server keeps no memory between them by default.
insights: Correct status codes let every tool (retries, caches, monitoring) behave correctly without reading your code.
Idempotent is about the effect on the server, not the response. DELETE /orders/5 twice may answer 204 and then 404, and it is still idempotent: the order is gone either way.
Header names are case-insensitive. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send them in lowercase, so code that looks for Content-Type with an exact, case-sensitive match will break.

prod.summary: In production, HTTP semantics are a contract with every machine between you and the user: browsers, CDNs, proxies, retry libraries and monitoring. Seniors check that methods and status codes are honest, that errors have a consistent body, that limits (header size, body size, timeouts) are known, and that retries cannot double-charge anyone.
checklist: Status codes match reality: 2xx only on success, 4xx for client mistakes, 5xx for server faults. Alerting is built on the 5xx rate, so a 200 with an error body hides outages.
Errors use one format, ideally Problem Details (application/problem+json, RFC 9457) with a stable type the client can switch on.
POST endpoints that create or charge accept an Idempotency-Key, so a retried request after a timeout does not run twice.
429 and 503 responses include Retry-After; clients back off instead of hammering.
Every response that can be cached sets Cache-Control on purpose; personalised responses say private or no-store.
Large cookies and JWTs are measured: headers have size limits at every proxy in the path.
GET handlers never change data (prefetchers, crawlers and link previews call them).
numbers: Node.js limits total request header size to 16 KiB by default (--max-http-header-size); bigger headers get 431.
Node.js server.headersTimeout defaults to 60 s and server.requestTimeout to 300 s; both answer with 408.
nginx default client_max_body_size is 1 MB; larger uploads get 413 Request Entity Too Large.
301/302 let clients change POST to GET on redirect; 307/308 keep the method and body.
failures: Customers are charged twice; logs show the same POST twice, 30 s apart.
The client (or a proxy) timed out and retried a non-idempotent POST that had actually succeeded. Accept an Idempotency-Key, store the first result, and return it for repeats.
Users with many cookies get 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large from nginx, or 431 from Node.
Cookies grew (tracking, big JWT sessions) past the header limit. Trim cookies, store sessions server-side, or raise large_client_header_buffers consistently at every hop.
Error dashboards look calm during an outage, but users complain.
The API returns 200 {"error": ...}, so the 5xx metric never moves. Return real status codes; alert on the 5xx rate and on p99 latency.
A form POST that hits a redirect arrives at the new URL as a GET with no body.
The server used 301/302, which clients historically turn into GET. Use 308 (permanent) or 307 (temporary) to keep the method and body.

code.title: Honest status codes and a race-free Idempotency-Key in a Next.js route handler
code.note: The key is claimed with one atomic insert backed by a unique constraint. A “find, then create” check lets two parallel retries both pass the check and create two orders. A real system also stores a hash of the body and rejects the same key with a different body. If the process crashes between claimKey and saving the order, the claimed row stays “in progress”: give claims a locked_at and let a retry take over after a timeout (or keep claim and order in one transaction).

qs.s: Your SPA's fetch wrapper retries any failed request up to 3 times. Which request is it unsafe to retry automatically after a network timeout?
o: POST /payments without an idempotency key
GET /orders/42
PUT /users/7/avatar with the full new avatar
DELETE /cart/items/3
qs.e: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating them leaves the same state. A POST that charges a card may have succeeded before the timeout; retrying it can charge twice unless the server deduplicates by an idempotency key.

qs.s: A client sends a valid JWT for user 15 and asks for GET /admin/reports, which only admins may see. User 15 is not an admin. Which status is correct?
o: 401 Unauthorized
400 Bad Request
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found is the only valid choice
qs.e: The server knows who the user is (authentication worked), and the user lacks permission: 403. 401 means “log in / your credentials are missing or invalid”. Some APIs return 404 to hide that a resource exists, but that is a deliberate privacy choice, not the default meaning.

qs.s: You read this in the logs: POST /api/upload 413 from nginx, and the request never reaches your Node app. Files under 1 MB work. What do you change?
o: Increase Node's requestTimeout
Raise nginx client_max_body_size for that location (and check the app's own body limit)
Switch the upload to GET
Add CORS headers
qs.e: 413 is “payload too large”, and nginx's default body limit is 1 MB, which matches the symptom. Raise it only on the upload route, and make sure the app's body parser allows the same size.

qs.s: Two people edit the same document. Read the traffic. What does the 412 mean, and what should the client do?

code.title: Optimistic concurrency
code.src:
GET /api/docs/7
-> 200 OK
   ETag: "v41"

PUT /api/docs/7
If-Match: "v41"
Content-Type: application/json
-> 412 Precondition Failed

o: The server is broken; retry the same PUT until it works
The ETag header is malformed; remove the quotes
The CDN has a stale copy; purge it
Someone else changed the document after you read version v41; fetch the new version, merge or ask the user, then retry with the new ETag
qs.e: If-Match says “apply this only if the document is still v41”. 412 means the current version is different, so the server refused to overwrite someone else's change (no lost update). Blindly retrying the same request gets 412 again, which is the point: the client must re-read first.

qs.s: Read this handler. Users say they were unsubscribed from the newsletter without clicking the link. What is happening?

code.title: unsubscribe.ts (Express)

o: The tokens are guessable
Email security scanners and link previews open GET links automatically, and this GET changes data
Express caches GET responses
The browser prefetches all links in an email client
qs.e: GET must be safe: many systems (mail scanners, preview bots, prefetchers) call GET URLs without a human. Show a confirmation page on GET and change data only on POST (RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe also uses a POST). Guessable tokens would be a different bug with a different symptom.

qs.s: nginx access log for a search API. Many lines look like this. What does 499 tell you?

code.title: access.log (custom format with rt/urt)
code.src:
10.0.3.17 "GET /api/search?q=phone HTTP/1.1" 499 0 rt=12.001 urt=12.001
10.0.3.17 "GET /api/search?q=laptop HTTP/1.1" 499 0 rt=12.000 urt=11.999
10.0.3.22 "GET /api/search?q=case HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 rt=0.420 urt=0.418

o: The upstream app returned status 499
nginx rate-limited the client
The client closed the connection before nginx had a response, here after 12 s (a client timeout shorter than the slow backend)
A bug in nginx; upgrade it
qs.e: 499 is nginx's own log code for “client closed request”; it is never sent on the wire. The steady 12 s suggests a client-side timeout, and urt (upstream time) equal to rt shows nginx was waiting for the upstream the whole time. The real problem is the slow search upstream. Note that the backend may keep working on requests nobody waits for: cancel work when the client disconnects.

qs.s: A mobile client retries PATCH /counters/9 with body {"op": "increment"} after a timeout, and the counter goes up by 2. A teammate says “PATCH is idempotent, so this cannot happen”. Who is right?
o: The teammate: all methods except POST are idempotent
Nobody; this is a database bug
The teammate, if HTTP/2 is used
The bug report: PATCH is not defined as idempotent. It depends on the payload. “Set field to X” is safe to repeat; “increment” is not
qs.e: RFC 9110 lists GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE as idempotent. PATCH is not in the list (RFC 5789). A JSON Merge Patch that sets values can be repeated safely; an increment cannot. Make it safe with an idempotency key or If-Match.

interview.q: Design the error contract for a public HTTP API. What status codes and what body?
answer: Status codes carry the class of failure: 400 malformed, 401 no/invalid credentials, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict with current state, 412 precondition failed, 422 validation, 429 rate limited, 5xx server faults. Clients, retry logic and alerting all depend on this.
One body format everywhere: Problem Details (RFC 9457, application/problem+json) with a stable type URI clients can switch on, a human title, and optional field errors.
Retry guidance: Retry-After on 429 and 503; document which errors are safe to retry.
Include a request ID in every response and log line so support can find the trace.
Never leak internals (stack traces, SQL) in 5xx bodies; never return 200 with an error inside.
followups: When would you return 404 instead of 403 on purpose?
How do you version error types without breaking clients?

interview.q: How do you make a POST that charges money safe to retry?
answer: The client generates an Idempotency-Key (UUID) per logical operation and sends the same key on every retry.
The server claims the key atomically (unique constraint / insert-if-absent), runs the operation, and stores the final response with the key.
Repeats with the same key return the stored response; a repeat while the first is still running gets 409 (or waits); the same key with a different body is rejected (422).
Keys expire after a window (for example 24 h) and are scoped per account.
Downstream calls (payment provider) also get an idempotency key, so the whole chain is safe, not only your API.
followups: What happens if your server crashes after charging but before saving the response?
Why is “check then insert” not enough?

interview.q: Explain 502, 503 and 504, and how you would debug each in a CDN → load balancer → nginx → Node setup.
answer: 502: a proxy got an invalid or no response from its upstream: crash, connection refused, reset, or a keep-alive race. 503: someone says “not available now”: no healthy targets, overload, maintenance. 504: a proxy gave up waiting for the upstream.
First find which hop generated it: response headers and body format (CDN error page vs nginx vs app), and each layer's logs.
For 502 in nginx, read the error log text: connect() failed (111) = app down, upstream prematurely closed connection = app closed the socket (crash or keep-alive timeout).
For 504, compare timeouts along the path; each outer timeout should be longer than the inner one, and slow work should become a background job.
Correlate with deploys, health-check changes and per-target metrics, not only the global error rate.
followups: Why can a low keep-alive timeout in Node cause 502s?
Should a client retry a 504?

one: HTTP wrapped in TLS: the traffic is encrypted and the server proves its identity with a certificate.
an: A sealed envelope plus a passport check. The certificate is the server's passport, stamped by an authority your browser already trusts.
how: During the TLS handshake the server sends its certificate chain. The browser checks that it leads to a trusted Certificate Authority, that the name matches the domain, and that it has not expired.

Public-key (asymmetric) crypto does two jobs: both sides agree on a shared secret (ECDHE key exchange), and the server signs the handshake to prove it owns the certificate's private key. Everything after that is encrypted with fast symmetric keys derived from the shared secret. In TLS 1.3 the key exchange is always ephemeral, so a key stolen later cannot decrypt traffic recorded earlier (forward secrecy).

TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for the handshake; resumed sessions can send data with zero round trips (0-RTT), but that early data can be replayed by an attacker, so it is only safe for idempotent requests. Certificates are short-lived (Let's Encrypt: 90 days) and getting shorter every year, so renewal must be automated. The exact dates are in the Production tab.
why: Without TLS anyone on the path (café Wi-Fi, ISP) can read and modify traffic, including passwords and cookies. Browsers also gate features like service workers and secure cookies on HTTPS.
trade: TLS termination: usually the load balancer or CDN decrypts, and traffic inside your private network may be plain HTTP. That is fine inside a trusted VPC, but zero-trust setups encrypt internal hops too (often via a service mesh with mTLS).

myth.m: HTTPS means the site is safe.
myth.r: It means the connection is private and you reached the domain you typed. A phishing site can have a perfectly valid certificate.

q.s: Your cert renewal cron silently failed and the site is down with certificate errors. What is the lasting fix?
o: Buy a 10-year certificate
Automate renewal and alert on certificate expiry ahead of time
Turn off HTTPS
Ask users to click through the warning
q.e: Short-lived certs are a feature. The fix is monitoring: alert when expiry is under, say, 14 days, so a broken renewal is caught while there is still time.

more: The certificate chain: leaf, intermediate, root, and why servers must send intermediates
SNI: how one IP serves many HTTPS domains
HSTS and the preload list
mTLS: clients also present certificates (service-to-service auth)
Certificate Transparency logs and how they expose mis-issued certificates
lab: Run openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -servername github.com </dev/null and find the certificate chain and the negotiated TLS version.
Inspect the certificate: ... | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates. Note the expiry date.
Search crt.sh for a domain you use and see every certificate ever issued for it.
Set up Caddy locally (it gets certificates automatically) or read how your host (Netlify, Vercel) renews them.
docs: Cloudflare Learning: What happens in a TLS handshake?

plain: HTTPS is HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel called TLS. It does two jobs. It hides the data from anyone in between (Wi-Fi owners, internet providers). And it proves the server is really the domain you typed, using a certificate signed by an organisation your browser trusts.
bridge: The padlock in the address bar is TLS. Netlify and Vercel give you certificates automatically through Let's Encrypt; that is why HTTPS “just works” when you add a domain there.

walk.title: What happens when you open https://bank.com
steps: The browser says “hello, I want bank.com” (this name is called SNI) and sends its half of a key exchange (a “key share”).
The server answers with its own key share. Both sides now compute the same secret key, without ever sending the key itself. From here on, everything is encrypted.
The server sends its certificate (“I am bank.com, signed by Let's Encrypt, valid until March”) and a signature that proves it holds the certificate's private key.
The browser checks: is the signer trusted? Does the name match? Is it expired? If any check fails, you see a full-page warning and nothing is sent.
The browser sends its request, encrypted with the shared key. Someone on the café Wi-Fi sees only noise. All of this took one round trip.

terms: A signed document proving a server owns a domain.
An organisation browsers trust to sign certificates.
The place where HTTPS is decrypted, often a load balancer or CDN.
insights: HTTPS proves you reached the domain, not that the domain is honest. Phishing sites have valid certificates too.
Expired certificates cause more outages than broken crypto. Automated renewal plus your own expiry alert is the real solution.
Many features (service workers, secure cookies, camera access) only work on HTTPS.

prod.summary: In production, TLS fails in boring ways: an expired certificate, a missing intermediate, a renewal job that stopped months ago, or an internal hop that nobody encrypted. Seniors automate renewal, monitor expiry from outside, know exactly where TLS terminates, and turn on HSTS only when every subdomain is ready for it.
checklist: Renewal is automatic (ACME: certbot, Caddy, cert-manager, or the platform), and renewal runs well before expiry (Let's Encrypt suggests at one-third of lifetime left).
An external monitor alerts when any public certificate has fewer than 14 days left. Do not rely on CA emails; Let's Encrypt stopped sending them in June 2025.
The server sends the full chain (leaf + intermediates). Test with openssl s_client or SSL Labs, not only in a browser that may have cached the intermediate.
TLS 1.2 is the minimum; TLS 1.0/1.1 are off. TLS 1.3 is on.
HTTP redirects to HTTPS with 308, then HSTS is sent (Strict-Transport-Security). Add includeSubDomains and preload only after checking every subdomain serves HTTPS.
The team knows where TLS terminates (CDN, load balancer, ingress) and whether the hop to the app is encrypted; the app trusts X-Forwarded-Proto only from that proxy.
Private keys are not in the repo or Docker image; they live in the platform's secret store.
numbers: CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081: maximum public certificate validity is 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027, 47 days from 15 March 2029.
Let's Encrypt: 90-day certificates now; default profile moves to 64 days on 10 February 2027 and 45 days on 16 February 2028.
TLS 1.3 full handshake: 1 round trip (TLS 1.2: 2). Resumption with 0-RTT: data in the first flight, but replayable.
HSTS preload list requires max-age of at least 31536000 (one year) plus includeSubDomains and preload.
failures: Site down with NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID on a Monday morning.

The renewal cron or ACME client failed weeks ago (DNS challenge broke, port 80 blocked, rate limit) and nobody noticed. Fix the renewal, then add an external expiry alert at 14 days so this is caught early next time.
Works in Chrome on your laptop, but Android apps, curl or Node clients fail with unable to verify the first certificate.
The server sends only the leaf certificate, not the intermediate. Desktop browsers sometimes fetch or cache the missing intermediate; other clients do not. Serve the full chain (fullchain.pem).
Login redirects loop forever between http:// and https:// after moving behind a load balancer.
TLS terminates at the balancer, so the app sees plain HTTP and keeps redirecting to HTTPS. Trust X-Forwarded-Proto from the balancer (for example Express app.set('trust proxy', 1)).
After enabling HSTS with includeSubDomains, an old internal tool on legacy.example.com is unreachable.
That subdomain only serves HTTP, and browsers now refuse it until max-age runs out. Roll out HSTS with a short max-age first, fix every subdomain, then raise it.

code.title: External certificate expiry check for a cron job or CI
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Exit 1 if any certificate expires within 14 days or cannot be fetched.
set -euo pipefail
DAYS=14
fail=0
for host in example.com api.example.com; do
  if ! cert=$(openssl s_client -connect "$host:443" -servername "$host" </dev/null 2>/dev/null); then
    echo "ALERT: $host: TLS connection failed" >&2
    fail=1; continue
  fi
  echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -subject -enddate
  if ! echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -checkend $((DAYS * 86400)) >/dev/null; then
    echo "ALERT: $host certificate expires within $DAYS days" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit "$fail"
code.note: -servername sends SNI, so you get the certificate for that host and not the server's default one. -checkend takes seconds. A host you cannot reach is an alert too: without that branch, set -e would end the script silently on the first unreachable host.

qs.s: You put Cloudflare in front of your server with TLS mode “Flexible” (HTTPS from browser to Cloudflare, plain HTTP from Cloudflare to your origin). Your app redirects all HTTP to HTTPS. What happens?
o: Everything works and the origin traffic is encrypted
An infinite redirect loop: the origin always sees HTTP and keeps redirecting
The browser shows a certificate name mismatch
Cloudflare caches the redirect and the site works after one minute
qs.e: The origin only ever receives plain HTTP from Cloudflare, so its HTTP→HTTPS redirect fires on every request, and Cloudflare follows the same path again. Use “Full (strict)” with a real origin certificate, or trust X-Forwarded-Proto.

qs.s: A mobile app team reports TLS errors only on some Android phones; browsers on desktop are fine. openssl s_client shows Certificate chain with one entry and verify error:num=21. What is wrong?
o: The certificate has expired
TLS 1.3 is not supported on Android
The domain name does not match
The server does not send the intermediate certificate
qs.e: Error 21 is “unable to verify the first certificate”, and a chain with only one entry means the intermediate is missing. Desktop browsers often fill the gap from cache; many clients do not. Serve the full chain.

qs.s: A senior proposes enabling TLS 1.3 0-RTT on the API to save a round trip for returning users. Which endpoint is the risk?
o: GET /products
GET /health
POST /transfers that moves money
Static image downloads
qs.e: 0-RTT early data can be captured and replayed by an attacker, so the server may see the same request twice. That is harmless for safe GETs but dangerous for a non-idempotent POST. CDNs that support 0-RTT usually limit it to safe requests or mark them with Early-Data: 1, so the app can answer 425 Too Early (RFC 8470).

qs.s: You test the origin directly, bypassing the CDN. Browsers through the CDN are fine. Why does openssl show the wrong certificate?

code.title: Checking the origin by IP
code.src:
$ openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.10:443 </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName
subject=CN = default.hosting-provider.net
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:default.hosting-provider.net

o: Connecting by IP sends no SNI, so the server returns its default certificate; add -servername api.shop.com
The origin certificate was issued for the wrong name
openssl does not support TLS 1.3
The CDN replaced the origin certificate
qs.e: One IP serves many HTTPS sites; the client names the site in the handshake with SNI. openssl sends SNI automatically only when you connect by host name. By IP, there is no SNI, so you get the default certificate. -servername (or curl --resolve) tests the real one.

qs.s: Read this fix a developer pushed to make calls to an internal service with a company-issued certificate work. What is the correct change?

code.title: billing-client.ts

o: It is fine inside a private network
Only remove the environment variable; rejectUnauthorized: false is safe
Trust the internal CA instead: connect: { ca: internalCaPem } or NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/ca.pem, and keep verification on
Switch the internal service to plain HTTP
qs.e: Turning off verification keeps encryption but removes identity: anyone who can intercept the traffic can present any certificate. The env variable disables it for the whole process, including calls to Stripe or your DB. The real problem is that Node does not know the internal CA, so give it that CA.

qs.s: Your mobile app pins the SHA-256 of the server's leaf public key. Ops renews the certificate every 60 days with a fresh key pair. What happens, and what is the safer design?
o: Nothing; pins follow the domain name
Only Android is affected
The app stops connecting after each renewal; pin a backup key and the CA/intermediate keys too (or skip pinning and rely on Certificate Transparency)
The renewal fails because of the pin
qs.e: A pin on the leaf key breaks as soon as the key changes, and users cannot reach you until they update the app. Shorter certificate lifetimes make this worse. If you must pin, pin keys that change rarely and keep a backup pin; many teams now avoid pinning entirely.

qs.s: Under CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081, what is the longest validity a publicly trusted TLS certificate issued on 1 April 2027 may have?
o: 398 days
200 days
47 days
100 days
qs.e: The limit dropped to 200 days on 15 March 2026 and to 100 days on 15 March 2027; it reaches 47 days on 15 March 2029. A certificate issued on 1 April 2027 falls in the 100-day period. Planning a manual yearly renewal is no longer possible.

interview.q: Walk me through a TLS 1.3 handshake. What does the certificate prove, and what does it not prove?
answer: ClientHello carries supported versions and ciphers, SNI (the host name) and a key share. ServerHello picks parameters and sends its key share; from here everything is encrypted.

The server sends its certificate chain and a signature over the handshake (CertificateVerify), proving it holds the private key, then Finished. The client verifies chain, name, dates, then sends Finished. One round trip in total.
Keys come from ephemeral ECDHE, so there is forward secrecy.
The certificate proves control of the domain at issuance time (domain validation). It does not prove the site is honest, the company is who you think, or that the server is not compromised.
Mention 0-RTT resumption and its replay risk, and that SNI is still visible on the wire unless ECH is used.
followups: What is the role of intermediate certificates?
How does revocation work, and why is it weak in practice?

interview.q: Where should TLS terminate in our architecture: CDN, load balancer or the app? What are the trade-offs?
answer: Terminating at the edge (CDN) gives the shortest handshake RTT for users, WAF and caching, but the CDN sees plaintext and you need a second, encrypted hop to the origin (“Full (strict)”, not “Flexible”).
Terminating at the load balancer centralises certificates and lets an L7 balancer route on paths and headers; the hop to the app is plain HTTP unless you re-encrypt.
End-to-end or mTLS between services (often via a service mesh) protects against an attacker inside the network and gives service identity, at the cost of certificate management and some CPU.
Wherever it terminates, the app must learn the original scheme and client IP from trusted forwarded headers only.
Compliance (PCI, HIPAA) often requires encryption in transit inside the network too.
followups: What is TLS passthrough at an L4 load balancer?
How does the app know the request was HTTPS?

interview.q: A certificate expired in production last month. Design the process so it cannot happen again.
answer: Automate issuance and renewal with ACME (cert-manager, Caddy, certbot, or the platform); renew at about one-third of the lifetime left.
Inventory every certificate, including ones outside the main platform: internal services, mobile API hosts, partner endpoints, CDN custom certs.
Monitor from outside: an external check alerts at 14–21 days left, independent of the renewal system (CA emails are not reliable; Let's Encrypt stopped sending them in 2025).
Alert on renewal failures themselves (ACME errors, DNS-01 challenge failures, rate limits), not only on expiry.
Run a blameless review: why the renewal broke silently, and add a test or a canary domain that renews often.
followups: Why are shorter certificate lifetimes a good thing?
HTTP-01 vs DNS-01 challenges: when do you need DNS-01?

one: Same semantics (methods, headers, status codes), different wire formats, each fixing the last one's bottleneck.
an: 1.1 is a single-lane road where one slow truck blocks everyone. HTTP/2 paints many lanes on the same road. HTTP/3 rebuilds the road so a crash in one lane does not stop the others.
how: HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per TCP connection. Browsers open about 6 connections per host to compensate. This is why old tricks like sprite sheets and domain sharding existed.
HTTP/2: binary, multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection, compresses headers (HPACK). But one lost TCP packet stalls every stream on that connection (TCP head-of-line blocking).

HTTP/3: runs over QUIC on UDP. Each stream recovers loss independently, the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes are merged into one round trip, and QUIC connection IDs allow a connection to survive a network change (Wi-Fi → 4G) where client and server support it.
why: It changes frontend performance advice. Under HTTP/2+, bundling everything into one giant file matters less, and splitting code into more, smaller chunks is cheap.
trade: HTTP/2 server push was dropped by browsers; preload hints and 103 Early Hints replaced it. HTTP/3 helps most on lossy mobile networks.

myth.m: HTTP/2 means I should stop bundling entirely.
myth.r: Request overhead dropped, but compression works better on bigger files and each request still has cost. Code-split by route, do not ship 800 tiny modules.

q.s: Your users are mostly on flaky mobile networks. Which protocol change most directly reduces stalls caused by packet loss?
o: Moving from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2
Enabling HTTP/3 (QUIC)
Adding more sprite sheets
Increasing DNS TTL
q.e: HTTP/2 still sits on TCP, so one lost packet blocks all streams. QUIC handles loss per stream, which is exactly the mobile problem.

more: HPACK and QPACK header compression
Stream prioritisation and why it was redesigned (RFC 9218)
103 Early Hints and <link rel=preload>
Connection coalescing across subdomains in HTTP/2
How CDNs advertise HTTP/3 via the Alt-Svc header
lab: Open DevTools → Network, right-click the column header, enable “Protocol”, and see h2/h3 per request on a few big sites.

Run curl -sI https://www.cloudflare.com | grep -i alt-svc and find the header advertising h3. Then run curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://www.cloudflare.com to see which version curl actually used.
Load a page on a throttled “Slow 4G” profile and compare the waterfall with and without many small requests.

plain:
HTTP has had three big versions. They mean the same thing (same methods, headers, status codes) but send it differently over the network.

HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection. HTTP/2 sends many requests at once over one connection. HTTP/3 does the same but over a newer transport (QUIC) that handles lost packets better, which helps a lot on mobile networks.
bridge: Old frontend tricks like sprite sheets, inlining everything, and bundling all JS into one file were workarounds for HTTP/1.1. With HTTP/2 and 3, splitting code into several smaller files is cheap.

walk.title: Loading 30 small files
steps: HTTP/1.1: the browser opens about 6 connections and sends 6 requests at a time. The other 24 wait in a queue. The waterfall looks like stairs.
HTTP/2: one connection, all 30 requests sent together, responses arrive mixed together. The waterfall is mostly flat.
On a phone, one packet gets lost. With HTTP/2 (on TCP), all 30 responses pause until that packet is resent.
HTTP/3 (on QUIC): only the one response that lost a packet pauses; the other 29 keep flowing.
You check the “Protocol” column in DevTools and see h2 or h3 per request.

terms: Sending many requests and responses at the same time over one connection.
One stuck item delaying everything behind it.
A transport built on UDP, used by HTTP/3.
Short names for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
insights: Your CDN or host usually decides the protocol. Check it rather than assume.
Split code by route, but do not go to extremes; hundreds of tiny files still cost something.
HTTP/3 helps most for users on mobile and unstable networks, a big share of users in many countries.

prod.summary: In production, the HTTP version is decided mostly by your CDN or load balancer on the client side, and often a different version is used between the proxy and your app. Seniors check what clients really negotiate, keep HTTP/1.1-era hacks out of new code, and know that HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 change which attacks and limits matter.
checklist: Check the real protocol per hop: browser → CDN (often h2/h3), CDN → origin (often HTTP/1.1 or h2), proxy → app. Each hop has its own limits and timeouts.
HTTP/3 is enabled on the CDN/edge and advertised with Alt-Svc; UDP 443 is open if you terminate QUIC yourself.
No domain sharding on HTTP/2+: it breaks connection reuse and costs extra DNS + TLS handshakes.
Server push is not used (browsers removed it). Use 103 Early Hints or <link rel=preload> for critical assets.
Your proxy/server is patched for HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (CVE-2023-44487) and has a sane max concurrent streams setting.
Code splitting is by route, not by hundreds of tiny modules; check the waterfall on a throttled mobile profile.
numbers: Browsers open up to 6 HTTP/1.1 connections per host.
HTTP/2 servers typically allow about 100 concurrent streams per connection (nginx http2_max_concurrent_streams default 128).
Cloudflare Radar 2025: about 21% of requests to Cloudflare used HTTP/3.
Chrome removed HTTP/2 server push in version 106 (2022).
failures: Users in some offices never get h3, even though the CDN supports it.
Their firewall blocks UDP 443, so the browser falls back to h2 over TCP. This is expected and harmless; make sure nothing depends on h3 being available.
After moving to HTTP/2, a page with one huge API response stalls other requests on a lossy network.
TCP head-of-line blocking: one lost packet pauses every stream on that connection. Enable HTTP/3 at the edge, and keep big responses paginated or streamed.
Server CPU spikes and many streams are opened and cancelled at once from a few IPs.
HTTP/2 Rapid Reset style attack. Update the server/proxy to a patched version, limit concurrent streams, and let the CDN absorb it.
SSE or long-polling breaks behind a proxy that talks HTTP/1.0 to the app.
Older nginx (before 1.29.7) used HTTP/1.0 to upstreams by default, which has no chunked encoding or keep-alive. Set proxy_http_version 1.1.

code.title: Checking which HTTP version each hop really uses
code.src:
# What did curl negotiate with the edge? (prints 1.1, 2 or 3)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://example.com

# Is HTTP/3 advertised?
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i '^alt-svc'
# alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400

# Force HTTP/3 (needs a curl built with HTTP/3 support)
curl --http3-only -sI https://example.com | head -1

# Bypass the CDN and ask the origin directly: which versions does it accept?
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' --http2 \
  --resolve example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://example.com
code.note: --resolve sends the request straight to the origin IP while keeping the right SNI and Host. The browser→edge and edge→origin protocols are often different.

qs.s: An old site still uses static1.example.com … static4.example.com to load assets faster. It now runs on HTTP/2. What is the effect of this sharding today?
o: It still speeds things up because each host gets 6 connections
No effect at all
It usually makes loading slower: extra DNS lookups and TLS handshakes, and requests cannot share one multiplexed connection
It is required for HTTP/3
qs.e: Sharding was a workaround for the 6-connections-per-host limit of HTTP/1.1. With HTTP/2, one connection carries all requests, so extra hostnames only add handshakes (unless the browser can coalesce them).

qs.s: A DevTools waterfall on HTTP/1.1 shows 30 small requests that start in groups of 6, like stairs. After moving the site to an HTTP/2 CDN, what do you expect?
o: Most requests start at about the same time on one connection
The same staircase, because the browser still limits to 6
Exactly one request at a time
Requests become UDP
qs.e: The staircase comes from the per-host connection limit. HTTP/2 multiplexes all requests over one connection, so they start together. HTTP/2 still runs over TCP, not UDP.

qs.s: Your product is used mostly on mobile networks with 2–3% packet loss. You already have HTTP/2. Which change most directly cuts stalls caused by loss?
o: Bundle all JavaScript into one file
Increase the HTTP/2 max concurrent streams
Add more domain shards
Enable HTTP/3 at the CDN so streams recover from loss independently
qs.e: Under HTTP/2, one lost TCP packet blocks all streams. QUIC handles loss per stream, so only the affected response waits. More streams or one big bundle do not change TCP's ordering.

qs.s: This nginx config has QUIC enabled, and curl --http3-only works from your office. Yet DevTools always shows h2 for real users. What is missing?

code.title: shop.conf

o: An Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 header, so browsers learn that HTTP/3 is available
UDP port 80 must be opened too
HTTP/2 must be turned off for HTTP/3 to work
A special QUIC certificate
qs.e: Browsers first connect over TCP and only switch to HTTP/3 after the server advertises it (with Alt-Svc, or an HTTPS DNS record). curl with --http3-only skips discovery, which is why it worked. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 run side by side with the same certificate.

qs.s: A page needs 24 small files from one host. RTT is 100 ms, each file fits in one round trip, server time is near zero, and the browser already has 6 open HTTP/1.1 connections. About how long until all files arrive? (Ignore bandwidth.)
o: About 100 ms
About 2,400 ms
About 400 ms
About 600 ms
qs.e: HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection: 24 files / 6 connections = 4 rounds × 100 ms = 400 ms. Over one HTTP/2 connection all 24 requests go out together, so about 100 ms. 2,400 ms would be a single connection.

qs.s: In 2026 a teammate wants to use HTTP/2 server push to send the critical CSS before the browser asks for it. What do you tell them?
o: Good idea; it is the standard way to speed up first paint
Use it, but only on HTTP/3
Browsers removed push (Chrome 106 in 2022); send 103 Early Hints with Link: rel=preload, or a preload tag in the HTML
Inline all CSS and JS into every HTML page instead
qs.e: Push was hard to use well (it often pushed files the browser already had cached) and was removed. 103 Early Hints lets the server tell the browser what to fetch while the HTML is still being generated, and the browser uses its own cache. Inlining everything kills caching across pages.

qs.s: gRPC calls through nginx fail. nginx logs upstream sent no valid HTTP/1.0 header and clients get INTERNAL: Received RST_STREAM. The config is below. What is the fix?

code.title: grpc.conf

o: Add proxy_buffering off
Use grpc_pass grpc://orders_grpc;: gRPC needs HTTP/2 (with trailers) to the backend too, and proxy_pass speaks HTTP/1.x by default
Turn on http3
Raise client_max_body_size
qs.e: http2 on only covers the client → nginx hop. Each hop negotiates its own version. gRPC requires HTTP/2 framing and trailers end to end, and nginx's gRPC module (grpc_pass) does that toward the upstream. Buffering is not the cause of a header error.

interview.q: What problem did HTTP/2 solve, and what problem did it leave that HTTP/3 solves?
answer: HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection; browsers open about 6 connections per host, and developers used sharding, sprites and bundling as workarounds.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, with binary framing and HPACK header compression, so one connection serves the whole page.
But TCP delivers bytes in order: one lost packet stalls every stream on that connection (transport head-of-line blocking). Under loss HTTP/2 can be worse than several HTTP/1.1 connections.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP: loss recovery per stream, TLS 1.3 built in (1-RTT setup, 0-RTT resumption), and connection IDs that can survive a network change.
Costs: UDP can be blocked (fallback needed), QUIC uses more CPU per byte in user space, and debugging tools are less mature.
followups: Why did server push fail?
What is HPACK and why did HTTP/3 need QPACK?

interview.q: Should we enable HTTP/3? How would you roll it out and measure the effect?
answer: Usually yes at the CDN or edge, where it is a setting; it helps most on mobile and lossy networks.
Roll out on the edge first, keep HTTP/2 as the fallback; confirm the Alt-Svc header and UDP 443 reachability.
Measure with real-user monitoring (RUM) split by protocol and network type: TTFB, LCP, error rate, not lab tests on fast Wi-Fi.
Expect only part of traffic to use it (Cloudflare Radar 2025: about 21% of requests), because of client support and UDP blocking.
If you terminate QUIC yourself: kernel UDP buffer tuning, load balancers that route by QUIC connection ID, and patching (QUIC stacks are newer code).
followups: Why does a load balancer need to know about QUIC connection IDs?
What does the first visit look like before the browser knows about h3?

interview.q: How does the HTTP version change your frontend bundling strategy?
answer: On HTTP/2+, many requests share one connection, so domain sharding and sprites are harmful or useless.
Split code by route and by rarely used features, so users download only what a page needs and caches survive deploys of other chunks.
Do not go to hundreds of tiny modules: each request still has header and scheduling cost, and compression works better on bigger files.
Use preload / modulepreload or 103 Early Hints for the critical chain, so the waterfall does not become deep.
Check the real waterfall on a throttled mobile profile, by protocol, before and after.
followups: What is a request waterfall and how do you flatten it?
How do content hashes interact with chunk splitting?
