one: A browser rule that lets a server say which other origins' JavaScript may read its responses.
an: A bouncer that only works inside browsers. The bouncer does not stop the request from leaving; it stops the page's JavaScript from reading the answer unless the server's guest list includes it.
how: An origin is scheme + host + port. https://app.com and https://api.app.com are different origins.
The same-origin policy blocks JS from reading cross-origin responses. CORS relaxes it: the server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming allowed origins.
"Non-simple" requests (custom headers, JSON content-type, PUT/DELETE) trigger a preflight: the browser first sends OPTIONS asking permission. If the answer is wrong, the real request never goes.
why: Without the same-origin policy, any website you visit could use your logged-in cookies to read your bank's API. CORS is the controlled way for a server to relax that policy for origins it trusts. A CORS error in the console is the browser protecting users; the fix is on the server (or in avoiding cross-origin calls), not in the frontend code.
trade: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * cannot be combined with credentials (cookies). Preflights add a round trip; Access-Control-Max-Age caches them. A same-origin setup (API behind /api on the same domain via a reverse proxy) removes CORS entirely.

myth.m: CORS protects my API from other servers and curl.
myth.r: CORS is enforced only by browsers. curl, Postman and any backend ignore it. It is not authentication.

q.s: A teammate "fixed" a CORS error by setting Allow-Origin to * on an API that uses cookie auth. Login still fails. Why?
o: Wildcard origins are not allowed with credentials
CORS does not support cookies at all
The DNS TTL is too high
They need HTTP/3
q.e: With credentials the server must echo the specific allowed origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The real fix may be serving the API same-origin.

more: Which requests are “simple” and skip the preflight
Access-Control-Expose-Headers: why your JS cannot read a custom response header
Vary: Origin when echoing origins, so caches do not mix answers
Local Network Access (Chrome 142+, replacing the older Private Network Access idea): public sites need the user's permission to call localhost or LAN addresses
Same-site vs same-origin (cookies use site; CORS uses origin)
lab: Run a page on localhost:5173 that fetches an API on localhost:3000 without CORS headers. Read the console error and the Network tab: note the request still reached the server.
Add Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173 and make it work.
Send a JSON POST and watch the OPTIONS preflight appear. Make the server answer it, then add Access-Control-Max-Age and watch the preflight disappear on repeat requests.
Finally, put the API behind a dev proxy (Vite server.proxy) so it is same-origin and the CORS headers are no longer needed.

plain:
By default, JavaScript on one website is not allowed to read responses from another website. This protects you: otherwise any site you visit could read your email or bank data using your logged-in cookies.

CORS is how a server says “I allow this other website to read my responses”. It is enforced only by browsers. The request often still reaches the server; the browser just hides the response from the page.
bridge: The red console error “blocked by CORS policy” when your app on localhost:5173 calls an API on localhost:3000 is this rule. Different port = different origin.

walk.title: Your frontend calls your API on another domain
steps: Page on app.shop.com runs fetch('https://api.shop.com/cart', { method: 'POST', headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'} }).
Because it is a JSON POST from another origin, the browser first sends a “preflight”: OPTIONS /cart asking “may app.shop.com send this?”
The API answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.shop.com and the allowed methods and headers.
The browser is satisfied and sends the real POST.
If the API had not answered the preflight correctly, the browser would never send the POST, and you would see a CORS error.

terms: The browser rule that blocks reading cross-origin responses by default.
An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before some cross-origin requests.
Cookies or auth sent with a cross-origin request; need extra CORS settings.
insights: When a browser shows a CORS error, open the Network tab, not only the console. Look at the OPTIONS response and the real response's status: the true problem is often a 401 or 500 without CORS headers.
A “simple” cross-origin request (for example a form POST) still reaches your server and still runs, even if the page cannot read the answer. That is why CORS does not replace CSRF protection.
The simplest fix is often to avoid cross-origin entirely: serve the API under /api on the same domain via a reverse proxy.

prod.summary: In production, CORS is a short allowlist of exact origins, answered the same way by the app and by every proxy or CDN in front of it. Seniors avoid cross-origin calls when they can (same domain via a reverse proxy), never reflect any origin with credentials, and make sure caches vary on Origin.
checklist: Allowed origins are an exact allowlist per environment (prod, preview, local), not a regex like .*example.com that also matches evil-example.com.
Never echo the request's Origin back blindly together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true: that lets any site read logged-in responses.
When the response depends on Origin, send Vary: Origin so a CDN does not serve one origin's CORS headers to another.
OPTIONS preflights are answered with 204 before auth middleware; auth on OPTIONS breaks every preflight.
Error responses (401, 500) also carry CORS headers, or the frontend sees a “CORS error” instead of the real status.
Custom response headers the frontend reads (X-Request-Id, pagination) are listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
CORS is not treated as access control: endpoints still check auth and CSRF.
numbers: Access-Control-Max-Age is capped at 7200 s (2 h) in Chromium and 86400 s (24 h) in Firefox; the default without the header is 5 s.
Chrome 142 (October 2025) started enforcing Local Network Access: requests from public sites to private IPs or localhost need user permission.
A preflight costs one extra round trip before the real request on every cache miss.
failures: The console says “blocked by CORS policy”, but the Network tab shows the API returned 500.
The error handler runs before (or without) the CORS middleware, so the 500 has no CORS headers and the browser hides it. Add CORS headers to error responses too, then fix the real 500.
Every request from the SPA fails preflight with 401 on OPTIONS.
Auth middleware runs on the preflight, but browsers never send credentials on OPTIONS. Answer OPTIONS before auth.

The CDN cached a response with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://admin.example.com and serves it to everyone. Add Vary: Origin or keep CORS responses out of the shared cache.
After enabling cookie auth, requests stop sending the session cookie cross-origin.

It breaks preflight caching
It only works on HTTP/2
Any website a logged-in user visits can read that user's API responses with their cookies
qs.e: Reflecting any origin with credentials is worse than *: browsers refuse * with credentials, but a reflected origin passes. An attacker's page can then call the API with the victim's cookies and read the results.

qs.s: A form posts JSON from app.shop.com to api.shop.com on every keystroke for autosave. DevTools shows an OPTIONS request before every POST. What reduces this most simply?

Send Access-Control-Max-Age on the preflight response, or serve the API under app.shop.com/api
Send the JSON with method GET
Turn off HTTPS on the API

fetch lowercases header names
Cross-origin JS can read only safelisted response headers unless the server lists others in Access-Control-Expose-Headers
The CDN strips custom headers
qs.e: For cross-origin responses, the browser exposes only a small safelist (like Content-Type). Add Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Total-Count. headers.get is case-insensitive, so lowercase is not the problem.

http://localhost:5173
None; the regex is correct
https://evilexample.com

A preflight must return 200, not 204
Content-Type is not allowed

qs.s: A team says: “Our API has a strict CORS allowlist, so we do not need CSRF protection for our cookie-based POST /transfer that accepts form data.” What is wrong with this?
o: Nothing; CORS blocks all cross-site requests
A form POST is a “simple” request: the browser sends it with cookies without a preflight. CORS only stops the attacker from reading the response; the transfer still happens
CSRF is only a risk for GET requests
CORS blocks the cookie, so CSRF is impossible

qs.s: To “fix” a CORS error, a developer adds mode: 'no-cors'. The error disappears from the console, but the next line fails. What happened?

no-cors disables CORS checks, so the JSON is just malformed
The partner API rejected the request
no-cors only works for POST

interview.q: Explain what CORS protects and what it does not protect.
answer: The same-origin policy stops scripts from one origin reading responses from another; CORS lets a server opt specific origins in.
It protects users: a malicious site cannot use their cookies to read data from your API in their browser.
It does not protect your API: curl, servers and scripts ignore it. Authentication and authorisation still do the real work.
It does not stop requests from being sent: simple requests reach the server and have side effects, so CSRF needs its own defence.
A wrong config can make things worse: reflecting any origin with credentials, or loose regexes, opens the API to any website.

interview.q: Our SPA on app.x.com calls api.x.com with cookie auth. What is needed, and what would you choose instead?
answer: Server: exact Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.x.com, Allow-Credentials: true, Vary: Origin, preflight answers for methods and headers used, Expose-Headers for headers the SPA reads.
Client: credentials: 'include' on every fetch.
Cookie: app.x.com and api.x.com are the same site, so SameSite=Lax works; across different sites you need SameSite=None; Secure, which third-party cookie restrictions increasingly block.
Cost: a preflight for most JSON requests (cache it with Max-Age).
Often better: serve the API same-origin under app.x.com/api through a reverse proxy; CORS disappears completely.

one: Ways to push data from server to browser without the user refreshing.
an: Polling is asking "anything new?" every few seconds. SSE is a radio broadcast you tune into. WebSockets are a phone line both sides can talk on.
how: Short polling: client requests every N seconds. Simple, wasteful, delayed. Long polling: server holds the request open until there is news.
Server-Sent Events: one long HTTP response that streams events, server → client only. Auto-reconnects, plain HTTP, works through most proxies. Used for LLM token streaming.
WebSockets: an HTTP request upgrades into a persistent two-way TCP channel. Good for chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing.
why: Picking the simplest one that fits saves real operational pain. Most "realtime" dashboards only need server → client, so SSE or even polling is enough.
trade: WebSockets are stateful connections: load balancers need to support them, deploys drop every connection, and horizontal scaling needs a shared pub/sub (e.g. Redis) so a message reaches users connected to other servers.

myth.r: Notifications and live feeds are one-way. SSE or polling with a sensible interval is often simpler and scales with ordinary HTTP infrastructure.

q.s: You run 4 chat servers behind a load balancer. User A (on server 1) messages user B (on server 3) and B never receives it. What is missing?
o: HTTPS
A shared pub/sub layer so servers can relay messages to each other
A bigger server
A longer DNS TTL
q.e: Each WebSocket lives on one server. Servers must publish messages to a shared channel (Redis pub/sub, NATS, Kafka) so whichever server holds B's socket can deliver.

Reconnect with backoff and resuming from the last event ID (SSE Last-Event-ID)
Proxy and load-balancer idle timeouts killing long-lived connections
Presence (who is online) and its consistency problems
WebTransport as a newer option

plain:
Normally the browser asks and the server answers. For live updates (chat, notifications, live prices), the server needs a way to tell the browser something without being asked.

Three options: polling (the browser asks every few seconds), Server-Sent Events (one long response the server keeps writing to), and WebSockets (a two-way connection that stays open).
bridge: When ChatGPT or Claude shows an answer word by word, that is usually Server-Sent Events. A live multiplayer game or collaborative editor typically uses WebSockets.

walk.title: Choosing for a “new order” notification badge
steps: Requirement: admins see a red badge within a few seconds when an order arrives. Only the server sends updates.
Polling every 10 seconds: simplest, works everywhere, but most requests return “nothing new”.
SSE: the browser opens new EventSource('/api/events'); the server writes data: {...} when an order arrives. One direction, plain HTTP, auto-reconnects.
WebSockets would also work, but you would need two-way support you do not need, plus more infrastructure.
You pick SSE. When you later run 3 servers, you add Redis pub/sub so an order created on server 1 reaches admins connected to server 2.

terms: Asking the server repeatedly on a timer.
A one-way stream of events from server to browser over HTTP.
A long-lived two-way connection between browser and server.
A message bus so many servers can broadcast to each other.
insights: Pick the simplest option that meets the need. Most “real-time” features are one-way.
Long-lived connections break on every deploy and every network change. Build reconnect logic from day one.
With more than one server, real-time always needs a shared channel (Redis, NATS) between servers.

prod.summary: In production, long-lived connections are the hard part, not the protocol. Every proxy, load balancer and deploy can cut them. Seniors design for reconnects (with resume from the last event), heartbeats under every idle timeout, a pub/sub layer between servers, and a limit on how many connections one instance holds.
checklist: The client reconnects with exponential backoff and jitter, and resumes from the last event ID, so a deploy does not cause a reconnect storm or lost messages.
Heartbeats (SSE comment lines or WebSocket pings) are sent more often than the shortest idle timeout in the path (nginx 60 s, AWS ALB 60 s by default).
Proxies do not buffer the stream: nginx proxy_buffering off or the X-Accel-Buffering: no header for SSE; WebSockets get the Upgrade/Connection headers.
Messages fan out through a shared pub/sub (Redis, NATS) so a user connected to server B gets events produced on server A.
The source of truth is still the database; the realtime channel is a hint. After reconnect the client refetches the current state.
SSE is served over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, or the app opens only one stream per tab, because of the HTTP/1.1 connection limit.
Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, stop accepting, tell clients to reconnect elsewhere, then close.
numbers: Over HTTP/1.1, browsers allow only 6 connections per domain across all tabs, so 6 open SSE tabs block every other request to that domain (MDN). Over HTTP/2 the limit is the stream limit, often 100.
nginx closes a proxied WebSocket that sends no data for 60 s (proxy_read_timeout default).
AWS ALB default idle timeout is 60 s, and it applies to WebSocket connections too.
SSE retry: sets the browser's reconnect delay in milliseconds.
failures: WebSocket connections drop exactly every 60 seconds when the chat is quiet.
The proxy or load balancer idle timeout (60 s default in nginx and ALB) closes connections with no traffic. Send a ping every 20–30 s, or raise the timeout for that route.
SSE works locally, but in production events arrive in big batches every few seconds, or only when the stream ends.
A proxy or compression layer buffers the response. Disable buffering (X-Accel-Buffering: no, proxy_buffering off), do not gzip the stream, and flush after each event.
After a deploy, Redis and the API spike to 10× normal load for a minute.
All clients lost their connection at once and reconnected (and refetched) at the same moment. Add jittered backoff, and roll instances one by one with connection draining.
Users with several tabs open say the app “freezes” and normal API calls hang.
Each tab holds an SSE stream over HTTP/1.1 and the browser's 6-connection limit per domain is used up. Serve over HTTP/2, or share one stream between tabs with a SharedWorker or BroadcastChannel.

qs.s: You stream LLM answers over SSE. Locally the text appears word by word. Behind nginx in production, the whole answer appears at once at the end. What is the most likely cause?
o: nginx buffers the proxied response; disable buffering for that route
SSE does not work over HTTPS
The browser limits SSE to 6 events
The LLM is slower in production
qs.e: nginx buffers upstream responses by default (proxy_buffering on), so tokens are held until the buffer fills or the response ends. Send X-Accel-Buffering: no or set proxy_buffering off.

qs.s: A stock dashboard shows prices that update once per second, server to client only, for 50,000 viewers. It runs on a normal HTTP/2 CDN + stateless API. Which option is usually the best fit?
o: WebSockets, because realtime always needs them
Short polling every 100 ms
Server-Sent Events, which are one-way, plain HTTP and auto-reconnect
A UDP socket from the browser
qs.e: The data flows one way, so the two-way channel of WebSockets adds stateful infrastructure for no gain. Polling every 100 ms would be 500,000 requests per second. Browsers cannot open raw UDP sockets.

qs.s: Your WebSocket chat runs on 3 servers with Redis pub/sub. During a deploy, server 2 restarts. Its users reconnect to servers 1 and 3. Some messages sent during those 5 seconds are missing. What fixes it?
o: Sticky sessions on the load balancer
Store messages durably and have clients fetch everything after their last seen message ID on reconnect
A longer Redis TTL
Switching from WebSockets to SSE
qs.e: Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget: a message published while a client is disconnected is gone. Persist messages (DB or a stream such as Redis Streams) and resume by ID. Sticky sessions do not help when the server itself restarts.

qs.s: Read this broadcast loop. Memory of the WebSocket server grows until it is OOM-killed, but only on days with many users on slow mobile networks. Why?

code.title: broadcast.ts (ws package)

o: JSON.stringify leaks memory
wss.clients keeps closed sockets forever
Slow clients cannot read as fast as you send, so unsent data piles up in each socket's buffer; check client.bufferedAmount and skip, coalesce or disconnect slow clients
WebSockets need a heartbeat to free memory
qs.e: send() never blocks; it queues. A client that reads slowly makes the queue grow without limit. This is backpressure. For state like prices, drop old updates for slow clients and send only the latest; above a limit, close the connection so the client reconnects and refetches.

qs.s: After each deploy, 50,000 clients reconnect, and the API and Redis fall over for a minute. Here is the client code. What is the fix?

code.title: socket.ts (browser)

o: Use exponential backoff with random jitter (for example up to 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … capped at 30 s, each randomised), and roll the deploy gradually
Reconnect immediately with no delay
Lower the delay to 100 ms so clients spread out
Switch to SSE, which never reconnects
qs.e: A fixed 1 s delay makes every client come back at the same moment, and again every second while the server is struggling (a thundering herd). Random jitter spreads them out; backoff reduces pressure while the server is down. SSE also reconnects, so switching protocol alone does not help.

qs.s: An admin dashboard is open on 20,000 screens and polls GET /api/stats every 5 seconds. How many requests per second does that create, and what is a cheap first improvement?
o: 400 req/s; nothing to improve
4,000 req/s; serve it from a short shared cache (or answer 304 via ETag) and poll less often when the tab is hidden
100,000 req/s; you must move to WebSockets
4,000 req/s; add sticky sessions
qs.e: 20,000 / 5 s = 4,000 requests per second, all asking for the same data. A 2–5 s shared cache makes almost all of them cheap hits; ETag/304 saves the body; the Page Visibility API stops polling in background tabs. Moving to a push channel is an option, not a requirement.

qs.s: Your SPA uses a Bearer token in the Authorization header for REST calls. Now you add a WebSocket. How do you authenticate it from the browser?
o: Pass { headers: { Authorization } } to new WebSocket()
WebSockets are always anonymous
Rely on CORS to block other sites
The browser API cannot set custom headers: use the session cookie (and check the Origin header on upgrade), or a short-lived single-use ticket sent in the URL or the first message
qs.e: new WebSocket(url, protocols) has no headers option. Cookies are sent on the upgrade request, but then any site can open a socket with them (cross-site WebSocket hijacking), and CORS does not apply to WebSockets. So check Origin, or use a short-lived ticket that leaks little if logged.

interview.q: Design live notifications for 1 million users. Polling, SSE or WebSockets?
answer: Start from the data flow: notifications are server → client only, latency of a few seconds is fine, so SSE (or long polling) fits; WebSockets add two-way state you do not need.

Connections: 1M concurrent long-lived connections need many instances (tens of thousands per Node process is realistic), raised file-descriptor limits, and load balancers with long idle timeouts plus heartbeats.
Fan-out: a pub/sub layer (Redis, NATS, Kafka) keyed by user, so the instance holding the user's connection receives the event.
Reliability: events stored durably with IDs; clients resume with Last-Event-ID and refetch state; the notification list in the DB stays the source of truth.
Mobile apps and closed tabs need push notifications (APNs/FCM/Web Push) anyway; the live channel is for open sessions.
followups: How do you handle a user with 5 open tabs?
What changes if users also send messages?

interview.q: How do you scale WebSockets horizontally and deploy without losing messages?
answer: Each socket lives on one instance; a shared pub/sub lets any instance deliver to any user. Track presence with TTL keys, not in memory.
Balance on connection count (least connections), cap connections per instance, and add a max connection age so load evens out after scaling.
Deploys: stop accepting new connections, tell clients to reconnect (close code 1012 “service restart”), drain gradually so clients spread over the remaining instances.
Clients reconnect with jittered backoff and resume from the last message ID; messages are stored (DB or streams), because plain pub/sub drops anything sent while a client is away.
Handle backpressure: per-socket buffer limits, drop or coalesce for slow clients.
followups: Why do sticky sessions not solve message loss?
How would you test a reconnect storm?

interview.q: How do you guarantee a client does not miss events while it is reconnecting?
answer: Give every event a monotonically ordered ID within its stream (DB sequence, Redis Streams ID, Kafka offset).
Persist events for a retention window, not only publish them.
On reconnect the client sends its last seen ID; the server subscribes first, replays everything after that ID, then flushes live events, removing duplicates.
If the gap is older than retention, tell the client to do a full refetch of current state.
The client is idempotent: applying the same event twice does nothing, so at-least-once delivery is safe.
followups: Why subscribe before replaying?
How long should retention be?

one: A worldwide network of cache servers that serve your files from a location near each user.
an: Instead of shipping every book from one warehouse in Seoul, you keep copies in small shops in every city.
how: DNS (or anycast routing) sends the user to the nearest edge server (point of presence). If the edge has the file cached, it answers immediately: a cache hit.
On a miss, the edge fetches from your origin server, stores it according to your Cache-Control headers, and serves the next users from cache.
Modern CDNs also terminate TLS, absorb DDoS attacks, and run code at the edge (Cloudflare Workers, Netlify/Vercel edge functions).
why: Latency is distance. A user in Tashkent hitting a server in Virginia pays ~200ms per round trip. A nearby edge cuts that to tens of ms and removes load from your origin.
trade: The hard part is invalidation. Fingerprinted filenames (app.3f9a2c.js) let you cache static files for a year; HTML stays short-lived. Caching personalized responses at the CDN can leak one user's data to another.

myth.m: A CDN is only for images.
myth.r: It can cache any response, including API GETs, HTML and whole static sites. Netlify and Vercel are essentially a CDN with a build step.

q.s: After a deploy, some users still get the old JavaScript for hours. Filenames are app.js and styles.css with Cache-Control: max-age=86400. Best fix?
o: Purge the CDN after every deploy forever
Use content-hashed filenames with long cache, and keep HTML short-cached
Disable the CDN
Set max-age=0 on everything
q.e: Hashed filenames change when content changes, so a new deploy produces new URLs. HTML (which references them) stays short-cached so it picks up the new names.

Origin shield / tiered caching to protect the origin
Purging by URL, by tag (surrogate keys) and by prefix
Signed URLs and cookies for private content
Image CDNs: on-the-fly resizing and format negotiation (AVIF/WebP)

docs: Cloudflare Learning: What is a CDN?

plain:
A CDN is a network of servers spread around the world that keep copies of your files. A user gets files from the nearest copy instead of from your one main server far away.

The first user in a region causes the CDN to fetch the file from your server (a miss). Everyone after gets it from the nearby copy (a hit) until it expires.
bridge: Netlify and Vercel are CDNs with a build step on top. When you deploy a React app there, your JS, CSS and images are copied to locations around the world automatically.

walk.title: A user in Seoul loads your site hosted in Frankfurt
steps: Without a CDN: every file travels from Frankfurt, about 250ms per round trip.
With a CDN: DNS sends the user to the Seoul edge server.
The first visitor requests app.4f3a1c.js. Seoul does not have it yet, fetches it from Frankfurt once, stores it.
Every later visitor in Korea gets it from Seoul in about 10ms.
Because the filename contains a content hash, the CDN can keep it for a year. A new deploy creates a new filename, so nobody gets stale code.

terms: A CDN server location near users.
Your real server, where the CDN fetches files on a miss.
Served from the CDN's copy / had to go to the origin.
Telling the CDN to delete its copy now.
insights: Long cache for hashed files, short cache for HTML. This one rule prevents most “users see old version” bugs.
Never let a shared CDN cache personal pages unless the cache key includes the user. Otherwise one user's page is shown to others.
CDNs also absorb attacks and traffic spikes that would knock over your origin.

prod.summary: In production, a CDN is a shared cache in front of your origin, so its biggest risks are serving stale content and serving one user's content to another. Seniors design the cache key and Cache-Control headers on purpose, measure the hit ratio, and know how to purge in seconds when something wrong is cached.
checklist: Hashed static assets: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. HTML: short or revalidated. API: explicit per route.
Personalised or authenticated responses send private or no-store; check that the CDN does not ignore it through an override rule.
The cache key is understood: which query strings, headers and cookies vary the response. Tracking parameters (utm_*) are stripped so they do not split the cache.
The cache hit ratio is on a dashboard; a sudden drop usually means a header change or a new query parameter.
Purge is scripted (by URL or by tag) and part of the deploy or CMS publish flow, not a manual dashboard click.
The origin only accepts traffic from the CDN (IP allowlist or a secret header), so attackers cannot bypass the CDN's protection.
stale-while-revalidate / stale-if-error are set where serving slightly old content is better than an error.
numbers: Cloudflare does not cache HTML or JSON by default, and skips caching responses that contain Set-Cookie.
Cloudflare's maximum cacheable file size is 512 MB on Free, Pro and Business plans.
max-age=31536000 = one year, the usual value for content-hashed files.
failures: A user reports seeing another user's name and cart on the homepage.

A personalised HTML response was cached at the CDN (for example a “cache everything” rule with no cookie in the key). Purge at once, send Cache-Control: private on personalised pages, and never cache responses that depend on cookies without varying on them.
After a deploy, the page is blank for some users; the console shows 404 for main.4f3a1c.js.
The cached HTML still references the old hashed files, which the deploy deleted. Keep old assets for a while after each deploy (most platforms do this), and keep HTML short-cached.
The origin falls over during a traffic spike even though the CDN “caches everything”.

Each URL variant (query strings, Vary: User-Agent, cookies) is a separate cache entry, so the hit ratio is low; or many edges miss at once. Normalise the cache key, remove useless Vary headers, and enable tiered caching / origin shield.
cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC or BYPASS on files you expected to be cached.

The response is not eligible: a Set-Cookie header, Cache-Control: private/no-store, or a file type the CDN does not cache by default. Remove the cookie from static responses or add an explicit cache rule.

code.title: Cache headers for the three kinds of responses
code.src:
# 1. Content-hashed asset: cache forever, the URL changes when content changes
GET /assets/app.4f3a1c.js
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# 2. HTML: browsers revalidate every time, the CDN may keep it 60 s
GET /products
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

# 3. Personalised API response: never in a shared cache
GET /api/me
Cache-Control: private, no-store

# Checking the CDN's decision
# $ curl -sI https://shop.com/assets/app.4f3a1c.js | grep -iE 'cache-status|^age|x-cache'
# cf-cache-status: HIT
# age: 5321
code.note: s-maxage applies only to shared caches such as CDNs. age shows how many seconds the CDN copy has existed.

qs.s: Your product listing API is the same for all users, changes a few times per hour, and gets 2,000 requests per second. The team sets Cache-Control: no-store “to be safe”. What do you suggest?
o: Keep no-store; APIs must never be cached
A short shared cache like s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60, so the origin sees about one request per 30 s per edge
max-age=31536000, immutable
private, max-age=3600
qs.e: The data is public and slightly stale data is acceptable, so a short CDN cache removes almost all origin load. immutable for a year would show old prices for a year. private only caches in each browser, so the origin still gets every first request.

qs.s: You run curl -sI on your hashed JS file many times and never see cf-cache-status: HIT. Every response has a Set-Cookie: session=... header. What is the likely reason it never caches?
o: The file is too small to cache
Cloudflare only caches over HTTP/3
The TTL is too long
The origin sends Set-Cookie on static files, which makes the response uncacheable by default
qs.e: Cloudflare will not cache a response with Set-Cookie by default, because the cookie may belong to one user. Stop the session middleware from running on static asset routes.

qs.s: Legal asks you to remove an image from the site within 10 minutes. It is served as /img/team.jpg with max-age=86400, through a CDN. What do you do?
o: Delete it at the origin and purge that URL on the CDN; browsers that already have it may still show it until their cache expires
Delete it at the origin; the CDN will notice immediately
Change the TTL to 0 and wait
Rename the HTML file
qs.e: The CDN keeps its copy until the TTL ends unless you purge it. Browser caches cannot be purged remotely, so be honest about that part. Changing the TTL does not affect copies already cached.

qs.s: Your CDN honours Vary. The product pages are public and the same for everyone, but the cache hit ratio is 8%. A typical response looks like this. What is the most likely cause?

code.title: curl -sI https://shop.com/products/42
code.src:
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
cache-control: public, max-age=300
vary: User-Agent, Accept-Encoding
x-cache: MISS

o: Vary: User-Agent splits the cache into one entry per browser version string, so most requests miss
max-age=300 is too short to cache
HTML can never be cached by a CDN
HTTP/2 disables caching
qs.e: There are thousands of distinct User-Agent strings, and each one becomes its own cache entry. Remove Vary: User-Agent (or normalise it into a few device classes at the edge). Accept-Encoding is fine because CDNs normalise it to a few values. Some CDNs, such as Cloudflare, ignore most Vary values instead.

qs.s: A deploy script sets these headers. What will happen after the next deploy?

code.title: headers config
code.src:
/index.html
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
/assets/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

o: Nothing bad; purging the CDN after each deploy fixes everything
Browsers that already have index.html keep the old version for up to a year, and it points to old asset files; a CDN purge cannot clear browser caches
Only the assets will be stale
The CDN refuses to cache HTML with immutable
qs.e: The HTML is the entry point, and it has no content hash in its URL. With a one-year browser cache users never ask for the new one. Hashed assets can be immutable; HTML needs max-age=0 (or no-cache) with revalidation, and at most a short s-maxage for the CDN.

qs.s: Traffic is 10,000 requests per second. The CDN hit ratio drops from 95% to 80% after a release added a random ?v= parameter to some URLs. By how much does origin load grow?
o: About 1.15×
About 15×
No change, the hit ratio only affects latency
About 4×
qs.e: Misses go to the origin: 5% of 10,000 = 500 req/s before, 20% = 2,000 req/s after, so 4× the load. Small changes in hit ratio near 100% have large effects on the origin. Strip or normalise useless query parameters in the cache key.

qs.s: Your site is behind a CDN with a WAF. An attacker finds the origin's IP in old DNS history and sends traffic straight to it. What is the right fix?
o: Change the DNS TTL
Turn on HTTPS on the origin
Make the origin accept traffic only from the CDN: firewall to the CDN's IP ranges plus authenticated origin pulls (mTLS) or a secret header, or a tunnel with no public IP
Purge the CDN cache
qs.e: The WAF and DDoS protection only cover traffic that passes through the CDN. If the origin answers anyone, it can be attacked directly. IP allowlists alone are weak on shared CDNs (another customer's traffic comes from the same ranges), so combine them with authentication, or use a tunnel and also rotate the origin IP.

interview.q: How would you set caching headers for a typical SPA or Next.js app: static assets, HTML and API?
answer: Content-hashed assets: public, max-age=31536000, immutable; a new build means new URLs, so they never need purging.
HTML: browsers revalidate (max-age=0 or no-cache with ETag); the CDN may keep it briefly (s-maxage) with stale-while-revalidate, purged on deploy.
Public API data: short shared caching (s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60) where slight staleness is acceptable.
Personalised or authenticated responses: private or no-store, and no CDN rule that overrides it.
Keep old asset files available for a while after deploy, so pages loaded before the deploy can still lazy-load their chunks.
followups: What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
Where does stale-if-error help?

interview.q: A personalised page was cached at the CDN and shown to other users. Walk me through the incident response and the prevention.
answer: Contain first: purge the affected URLs (or everything), disable the rule that caused it, and confirm with curl from several locations that responses are now uncached.
Assess impact: which URLs, for how long, which data was exposed; this is a data incident, so involve security/privacy and follow notification rules.
Root cause: usually a “cache everything” rule, a missing private/no-store, or a cache key that ignores the session cookie.
Prevent: personalised routes send private, no-store by default (framework middleware), CDN rules are in code review, and a test asserts the headers on authenticated routes.
Design: split public and personal content (cache the shell, fetch user data from an uncached API).
followups: How do you cache a page that is 95% public and 5% personal?
How would you detect this automatically?

interview.q: How do you invalidate CDN content at scale?
answer: Prefer not to invalidate: versioned or hashed URLs make new content a new object.
Tag-based purge (surrogate keys / cache tags): tag responses with entity IDs (product-42) and purge by tag when the entity changes in the CMS or DB.
Short TTLs plus stale-while-revalidate for data that changes often, so users get fast responses and freshness within seconds.
Automate purge in the publish or deploy pipeline and log it; know the CDN's purge rate limits and propagation time.
Remember browser caches cannot be purged: keep browser TTLs short for anything that may need to change urgently.
followups: What is an origin shield and why does it help after a purge?
How would you purge after a bad deploy of HTML?

videos.t: What Is A CDN? How Does It Work?
videos.why: What a CDN is and how a request reaches the nearest edge.

one: A server that sits in front of your app servers, receives client requests, and forwards them on.
an: A hotel reception desk. Guests never walk into the kitchen or laundry; reception takes the request and routes it to the right department.
how: A forward proxy acts for clients (a corporate proxy). A reverse proxy acts for servers. Nginx, Caddy, HAProxy, Traefik and Envoy are common ones.
Typical jobs: TLS termination, routing by path or host (/api → backend, everything else → frontend), compression, static file serving, rate limiting, request buffering.
The client only ever sees the proxy's address; app servers can live on a private network.
why: It gives one front door where cross-cutting concerns live once instead of in every service, and it hides your internal topology.
trade: One more hop and one more thing to configure. Behind a proxy the app sees the proxy's IP, so it must trust X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto, but only from the proxy, or clients can spoof their IP.

myth.m: Reverse proxy, load balancer, API gateway are totally different products.
myth.r: They overlap heavily. A load balancer is a reverse proxy that spreads load; an API gateway is a reverse proxy with API features (auth, quotas, keys).

q.s: Your rate limiter behind Nginx blocks all users at once after one abuser shows up. Likely cause?
o: Nginx is too slow
The app keys rate limits on the connection IP, which is always the proxy's IP
DNS caching
HTTP/2 multiplexing
q.e: Every request arrives from the proxy, so everyone shares one bucket. Use the client IP from X-Forwarded-For, trusting it only from your proxy.

more: Buffering, timeouts (connect, read, send) and body size limits
WebSocket proxying (Upgrade headers)
The Forwarded / X-Forwarded-* headers and trusted proxy lists
Gzip/brotli at the proxy
Config reload without dropping connections
lab: Run nginx in Docker in front of two local apps: / → frontend on 5173, /api → backend on 3000.
Add a 1MB client_max_body_size and try uploading a bigger file. Read the 413.
Log $remote_addr and $http_x_forwarded_for and see what your app receives.
Swap nginx for Caddy and compare the config size.
docs: Cloudflare Learning: What is a reverse proxy?

plain:
A reverse proxy is a server that stands in front of your app servers. Users talk only to the proxy. The proxy decides which internal server should handle each request, passes it on, and returns the answer.

It is a natural place for shared jobs: HTTPS, compression, routing /api to the backend and everything else to the frontend, size limits, rate limits.
bridge: The server.proxy setting in Vite's config is a tiny reverse proxy: requests to /api on your dev server get forwarded to your backend, which also avoids CORS.

walk.title: One domain, two apps
steps: You have a React frontend (port 5173 in dev, static files in prod) and a Node API (port 3000).
You put nginx in front, listening on port 443 for shop.com.
A request for shop.com/products gets the frontend files. A request for shop.com/api/products is forwarded to localhost:3000.
nginx handles the HTTPS certificate, so the Node app only speaks plain HTTP on the private network.
nginx adds X-Forwarded-For with the user's real IP, because the app otherwise sees only the proxy's IP.

terms: A server in front of your servers, acting on their behalf.
A server in front of users, acting on their behalf (e.g. a company proxy).
Header where proxies record the original client IP.
The server the proxy forwards to.
insights: Load balancers and API gateways are reverse proxies with extra features.
Because the proxy is the only public entry, it is also the cheapest place for shared rules: HTTPS, compression, size limits and rate limits, written once instead of in every service.
Proxies have timeouts and body size limits. Many “random 413/504 errors” are proxy settings, not app bugs.

prod.summary: In production, the reverse proxy is where many “random” errors come from: timeouts, body size limits, buffering, and wrong client IPs. Seniors keep the proxy config in version control, set every timeout and limit on purpose, log the upstream timing, and make sure the app trusts forwarded headers only from the proxy.
checklist: Timeouts are set per route on purpose: proxy_connect_timeout, proxy_read_timeout (longer for uploads, reports, streaming), and they are shorter than the client's timeout.
Body size limits (client_max_body_size) match what the app accepts, per route.
The proxy sets X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and Host; the app trusts them only from the proxy's IP (Express trust proxy, nginx real_ip_from).
Access logs include $upstream_response_time and $upstream_status, so you can tell a slow app from a slow proxy.
Keep-alive to upstreams is on, so the proxy does not open a new TCP connection per request.
WebSocket and SSE routes have upgrade headers and no buffering.
Config is tested (nginx -t) and reloaded (nginx -s reload) without dropping connections.
numbers: nginx defaults: proxy_connect_timeout 60 s, proxy_read_timeout 60 s, client_max_body_size 1 MB, proxy_buffering on.
nginx used HTTP/1.0 to upstreams by default before 1.29.7; since 1.29.7 (March 2026) the default is HTTP/1.1 with upstream keep-alive on.

Node.js 22, 24 and 26: server.keepAliveTimeout defaults to 5 s, shorter than many proxies' upstream idle timeouts. A change of the default to 65 s was merged in April 2026 for the next major release (Node.js 27), so check the version you run.
failures: Report downloads fail after exactly 60 s with 504 Gateway Time-out from nginx.
proxy_read_timeout (default 60 s) fired while the app was still building the report. Raise the timeout for that location only, or make the report a background job the client polls.
Uploads above 1 MB fail with 413 Request Entity Too Large and the app logs nothing.
nginx rejected the body (default client_max_body_size 1m) before it reached the app. Raise the limit for the upload route.
Every user appears to come from 10.0.0.5 in logs, rate limits and geo-IP.
The app reads the socket address, which is the proxy. Configure the trusted proxy so the app reads the client IP from X-Forwarded-For, and only from that proxy.
Occasional 502 Bad Gateway with upstream prematurely closed connection in the nginx error log.

nginx reused an idle keep-alive connection that Node had just closed (Node's default keep-alive timeout is 5 s). Set the app's keepAliveTimeout longer than the proxy's idle time, or lower the proxy's keepalive_timeout for the upstream.

code.title: One domain, frontend + API + WebSocket, with explicit limits
code.note: On nginx older than 1.29.7 the two lines with comments in /api/ are required, otherwise every request opens a new upstream connection.

qs.s: Your Express app runs behind nginx. It decides “is this request HTTPS?” to set Secure cookies, but cookies are never marked Secure in production. TLS terminates at nginx. What is missing?
o: A new TLS certificate on the Node app
HTTP/2 between nginx and Node
nginx sending X-Forwarded-Proto and Express trusting the proxy (app.set('trust proxy', 1))
A bigger client_max_body_size
qs.e: The app only sees plain HTTP from nginx. It learns the original scheme from X-Forwarded-Proto, and Express uses it only when trust proxy is set. Adding TLS to the app is possible but is not the usual fix.

qs.s: nginx error log: upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream on /api/export, after 60 s. The app finishes in about 90 s. Best change?
o: Make the export a background job (or raise proxy_read_timeout only for that location)
Raise client_max_body_size
Raise proxy_connect_timeout
Turn off keep-alive
qs.e: The connection was made; nginx gave up waiting for the response header, which is proxy_read_timeout (default 60 s). proxy_connect_timeout covers only opening the connection. Long work is better as a job than a held request.

qs.s: A client sends X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4 directly to your app, which is behind nginx using $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for. The app reads the first IP in the header for rate limiting. What happens?
o: nginx removes the fake value
The app sees the client's real IP
The request is rejected with 400
The attacker chooses their own IP and can avoid rate limits
qs.e: $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for appends the real IP to whatever the client sent, so the header becomes 1.2.3.4, <real ip>. Read from the right, skipping only your trusted proxies (or use nginx real_ip with set_real_ip_from).

qs.s: Requests to /api/users reach the Node app as //users and get 404. What is the fix?

code.title: site.conf

o: Use location /api/ with proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000/; so /api/users becomes /users (or drop the trailing / in proxy_pass to keep /api/users)
Add proxy_http_version 1.1
Add rewrite ^ /users;
Set merge_slashes off
qs.e: When proxy_pass has a URI (here /), nginx replaces the matched location prefix with it: /api → /, so /api/users becomes //users. Make the location and the URI end the same way, or pass no URI so the path is forwarded unchanged.

qs.s: The API container is redeployed and gets a new IP. nginx keeps returning 502 with connect() failed (113: No route to host) until someone reloads it. Why?

code.title: api.conf

o: The DNS TTL of api.internal is too long
Docker networking is broken
nginx resolves host names in upstream once at startup and keeps the IP; use resolver, a zone in the upstream and server api.internal:3000 resolve; (or a variable in proxy_pass)
proxy_read_timeout is too short
qs.e: A static upstream server name is looked up only when the config loads, so the TTL never matters. With a resolver, a shared-memory zone (for example zone api 1m;) and the resolve parameter (open-source nginx since 1.27.3), nginx re-resolves the name while running. Without the zone, nginx refuses the config.

qs.s: A teammate wants to set proxy_buffering off globally “to reduce latency”. For a normal JSON API with many mobile users, what do you lose?
o: Nothing; buffering only matters for static files
TLS stops working
Upstream keep-alive is disabled
nginx no longer absorbs slow clients: each Node request stays busy (memory, a connection, maybe a DB transaction) until a slow phone has downloaded the whole response
qs.e: With buffering on, nginx reads the full response from the app quickly, frees the app, and then feeds slow clients itself. Turn buffering off only for streaming routes (SSE, LLM tokens), not globally.

qs.s: One of two API servers freezes: it accepts TCP connections but never answers. nginx uses default proxy_next_upstream settings. GET requests are slow but succeed; some POST requests fail with 504. Why the difference?
o: nginx never retries POST because of CORS
After a timeout, nginx retries the request on the next server only for idempotent methods; a POST that was already sent is not retried, because it might have run
POST bodies are larger, so they time out
GET responses are cached
qs.e: Since nginx 1.9.13, non-idempotent requests (POST, LOCK, PATCH) are not passed to the next upstream once they were sent, unless you add non_idempotent. That protects you from double execution. Fix the real issue with shorter timeouts, passive health checks (max_fails/fail_timeout) and idempotency keys.

interview.q: Which jobs would you put in the reverse proxy, and which in the application? Where is the line?
answer: Proxy: TLS termination, HTTP/2–3, compression, static files, routing by host and path, body size limits, timeouts, basic rate limits by IP, request IDs, access logs.
App: anything that needs business knowledge: authorisation, per-user or per-plan limits, validation, idempotency.
Grey zone: authentication (token validation at a gateway is fine, permission checks stay in the app), caching (proxy for public, app for personalised).
Keep the proxy config in version control and reviewed; the more logic it holds, the more it needs tests.
Avoid two layers doing the same job with different settings (two body limits, two timeouts) unless they are deliberately ordered.
followups: When does an API gateway make sense over plain nginx?
How do you test proxy config changes safely?

interview.q: Users get intermittent 502s from nginx. How do you investigate?
answer: Read the nginx error log message, it names the cause: connect() failed (111: Connection refused) = nothing listening (crash, deploy), upstream prematurely closed connection = app closed the socket (crash or keep-alive race), no live upstreams = all marked failed.
Use access logs with $upstream_addr, $upstream_status and $upstream_response_time to see which instance and how long.
Correlate with deploys, OOM kills and restarts of the app.
Check keep-alive ordering: the app's keep-alive timeout must be longer than nginx's upstream idle timeout.
Fix the cause, then add safety: graceful shutdown, passive health checks, retries for idempotent requests only.
followups: Why are 502s more frequent at low traffic with keep-alive races?
What is the difference between 502 and 504 in nginx?

interview.q: How do you get the real client IP safely through CDN → load balancer → nginx → app?
answer: Each hop appends the address it saw to X-Forwarded-For; the leftmost values are whatever the client sent and can be fake.
Read the header from the right and skip only hops you trust (known CIDRs of your CDN, LB and proxy); the first untrusted address is the client.
In nginx: set_real_ip_from for each trusted range plus real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For and real_ip_recursive on; in Express: trust proxy set to the hop count or the CIDRs, never true blindly.
Or use a header your edge sets and overwrites (for example CF-Connecting-IP), and block direct access to the origin so nobody can send it themselves.
Test it: send a fake X-Forwarded-For through the full chain and check what the app logs.
followups: What is the standard Forwarded header?
What breaks when you add a new proxy layer?

videos.t: Proxy vs Reverse Proxy Server Explained
videos.why: Backend engineer's take on what each proxy sees and can do.

one: Spreads incoming traffic across several servers and stops sending to ones that are unhealthy.
an: The person at the bank pointing each customer to the next free teller, and skipping the teller who went home sick.
how: L4 balancers route TCP/UDP connections by IP and port without reading the content: very fast. L7 balancers read HTTP and can route by path, header or cookie.
Algorithms: round robin, least connections, weighted, or hash-based (same user → same server).
Health checks call an endpoint like /readyz on a timer (AWS ALB: every 30 s by default); servers that fail are taken out of rotation automatically and come back after several passing checks.
why: It is what makes horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deploys possible: add servers behind it, drain old ones out of it.
trade: Sticky sessions (pin a user to one server) are a crutch for servers that keep state in memory. They break when that server dies and they unbalance load. Prefer stateless servers with state in a DB or Redis.

myth.m: The load balancer is a single point of failure, so it defeats the purpose.
myth.r: Managed balancers (AWS ALB, GCP LB) are themselves redundant across zones. Self-hosted ones run in pairs with a floating IP.

q.s: Users get logged out randomly since you went from 1 to 3 app servers. Sessions are stored in server memory. Best fix?
o: Sticky sessions forever
Move sessions to a shared store (Redis/DB) or a signed cookie so any server can handle any request
Go back to 1 server
Raise the health check interval
q.e: Sticky sessions hide the problem until a server restarts. Externalizing state makes servers interchangeable, which is what horizontal scaling needs.

Slow start for new instances
Global load balancing (GeoDNS, anycast) vs regional
L4 passthrough TLS vs L7 termination
Outlier detection: ejecting hosts that return many 5xx
lab: Put nginx (or HAProxy) in front of three copies of a tiny server that returns its own port. Hit it in a loop and watch round robin.
Add a /healthz to each and configure health checks (HAProxy makes this easy). Kill one copy and confirm traffic avoids it.
Store a counter in server memory, increment per request, and watch it make no sense behind the balancer. Move it to Redis.
docs: Cloudflare Learning: What is load balancing?

plain: When one server is not enough, you run several copies of your app. A load balancer sits in front of them and spreads requests across them. It also checks each copy's health and stops sending traffic to broken ones.
bridge: On Vercel or Netlify, your functions automatically run on many instances behind a balancer. When you self-host or use containers, you set this up yourself or the platform provides it.

walk.title: Deploying without downtime using a load balancer
steps: Three app instances (A, B, C) run behind the balancer. Each gets about a third of the traffic.
You start new instance D with the new version. The balancer calls its readiness endpoint /readyz until D answers 200, then starts sending it traffic.
You tell the balancer to drain A: no new requests to A, but let its current requests finish.
When A is idle, you stop it. Repeat for B and C.
Users never saw an error, because at every moment at least three healthy instances were serving.

terms: Send requests to servers in turn: A, B, C, A, B, C.
A regular request to see if a server is OK.
Stop sending new requests to a server but let current ones finish.
Always sending the same user to the same server.
insights: If logging in only works sometimes after you add a second server, sessions are stored in memory. Move them to Redis or the DB.
L7 (HTTP-aware) balancers can route by path or header; L4 ones only see IPs and ports but are faster.
Health checks that are too strict (checking the database) can remove every server at once during a small DB hiccup.

prod.summary: In production, a load balancer is only as good as its health checks and its timeouts. Seniors make health checks reflect “can this instance serve traffic”, line up idle timeouts so the balancer never reuses a closed connection, drain connections during deploys, and watch per-target error rates rather than the average.
checklist: Two endpoints: liveness (process is alive, no dependencies) and readiness (can serve, warm, connected). The balancer uses readiness.
Readiness does not fail just because a shared dependency (the database) is slow, or every instance leaves at once.
The app's keep-alive timeout is longer than the balancer's idle timeout (ALB default 60 s; Node default 5 s, so it must be raised).
Deregistration delay / connection draining is longer than your slowest normal request, and the app handles SIGTERM by finishing in-flight requests.
Metrics per target: 5xx count, latency, healthy host count. Alert when healthy hosts drop below what can carry peak traffic.
Sessions and uploads are not stored in instance memory or local disk; any instance can serve any request.
Slow start or warm-up is used for instances that need cache or JIT warm-up before full traffic.
numbers: AWS ALB defaults: health check every 30 s, timeout 5 s, healthy after 5 successes, unhealthy after 2 failures, success code 200.
AWS ALB default idle timeout is 60 s (range 1–4000 s). If the target closes idle connections first, the ALB can return 502.
Node.js 22, 24 and 26: server.keepAliveTimeout default is 5 s. A change to 65 s was merged in April 2026 for the next major release (Node.js 27), so check your version instead of assuming.
If all targets in an ALB target group are unhealthy, the ALB “fails open” and sends traffic to all of them anyway.
failures: A small, steady rate of 502 Bad Gateway from the ALB, with no errors in app logs.

Node closes idle keep-alive connections after 5 s, but the ALB keeps them for 60 s and sometimes sends a request on a socket Node just closed. Set server.keepAliveTimeout to about 65 s and headersTimeout a bit higher.
In Kubernetes, a 20-second database failover becomes a 2-minute total outage with 503 from the ingress.

The readiness probe queried the DB, so every pod failed at once and was removed from the Service; pods then need several passing probes to return. Keep shared dependencies out of readiness, or degrade instead of failing it. (An AWS ALB “fails open” when all targets are unhealthy, which hides this bug until you move platforms.)
During every deploy, a few users get 502/503 or broken uploads.
Instances are killed before in-flight requests finish. Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish current requests, then exit; set the deregistration delay longer than your slowest request.
One instance has a 30% error rate, but the overall dashboard shows only 3%.
Averages hide a bad host (bad disk, failed config). Watch per-target metrics and use outlier detection to eject hosts with many 5xx.

code.note: Closing idle sockets right at SIGTERM (before the LB stops routing) only makes the LB open new connections to a dying instance; do it after the wait. The last timer makes sure a stuck request cannot block shutdown past the grace period.

qs.s: In Kubernetes, every pod's readiness probe runs SELECT 1 on the shared Postgres. The DB has a 20-second failover. What happens to the site, and why?
o: Nothing; readiness probes ignore database errors
Only the pod closest to the DB fails
Pods restart, which fixes the DB connection faster
All pods become not-ready together and leave the Service, so a short DB blip becomes a longer, total outage
qs.e: A shared dependency makes every pod fail at once. Even after the DB is back, pods need passing probes before they get traffic again. A failing readiness probe removes the pod from traffic; it does not restart it (that is liveness). Probes should show whether this pod can serve.

qs.s: Behind an AWS ALB (idle timeout 60 s), a Node API with default settings shows about 0.1% 502 errors, more during low traffic. App logs are clean. Which change fixes it?
o: Lower the ALB idle timeout to 1 s
Set Node's server.keepAliveTimeout above 60 s (for example 65 s)
Enable sticky sessions
Add more instances
qs.e: Node's default keep-alive timeout is 5 s. The ALB reuses idle connections for up to 60 s and sometimes sends a request just as Node closes the socket. The app's timeout must be longer than the balancer's.

qs.s: A video-upload service keeps partly uploaded chunks on the instance's local disk. You move from 1 to 4 instances behind a round-robin balancer. What will users see, and what is the lasting fix?
o: Uploads fail when chunks land on different instances; upload directly to object storage (for example presigned S3 URLs) or a shared store
Nothing changes, round robin keeps a user on one instance
Uploads get 4× faster
The balancer merges the chunks automatically
qs.e: Round robin sends each request to a different instance, so chunks are split across disks. Sticky sessions hide it until an instance dies. Moving the state out of the instance makes all instances interchangeable.

qs.s: Read this Kubernetes probe config. The database has a 30-second slowdown. What happens to the pods?

code.title: deployment.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 3000 }  # /healthz runs SELECT 1
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 1
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 }
  periodSeconds: 5

o: Pods are only removed from the Service until the DB recovers
Nothing; probes ignore slow responses
Only one pod restarts, the others keep serving
After about 15 s every pod fails its liveness probe and is restarted, at the same time, making the outage longer and adding cold starts
qs.e: A failed liveness probe makes the kubelet restart the container, not just remove it from traffic. Because the probe depends on a shared DB, all pods fail together and restart in a loop. Liveness should only check the process itself; dependency problems belong in metrics and, carefully, in readiness.

qs.s: All traffic comes through a CDN. One of the three servers sits at 90% CPU while the other two are almost idle. Why?

code.title: upstream.conf

o: Consistent hashing is broken in nginx
Server 10.0.1.10 is faster, so it gets more

$remote_addr is the CDN edge's IP; a few edge IPs carry most traffic, so most requests hash to the same server. Use the real client IP or a session key, or plain least-connections if affinity is not needed
The CDN caches responses from only one server
qs.e: Hashing balances well only when the key has many different values. Behind a CDN there are only a few source IPs, often from the edge nearest your users. Hash on something with many values, or do not use affinity at all if servers are stateless.

qs.s: Each instance safely handles 500 req/s. Peak traffic is 1,800 req/s. You run instances evenly in 2 availability zones and must survive losing one whole zone at peak. What is the minimum number of instances?
qs.e: If a zone fails, the other zone alone must carry 1,800 req/s: 1,800 / 500 = 3.6, so 4 instances per zone, 8 in total. With only 4 total (2 per zone), the surviving zone has 1,000 req/s of capacity and falls over, which can then cascade.

qs.s: Your WebSocket service had 2 instances. You scale to 4 during a traffic spike. An hour later, the 2 old instances are still overloaded and the new ones are almost idle. The balancer uses least-connections. Why, and what helps?
o: Long-lived connections stay where they were opened; balancing only affects new connections. Add a max connection age (or ask some clients to reconnect) so load spreads out
Least-connections is broken; use round robin
New instances failed their health checks
WebSockets cannot be load balanced
qs.e: A load balancer decides once, when the connection opens. Existing sockets can live for hours, so old instances keep their load. Servers should close connections after a jittered maximum age, so clients reconnect and land on the less-loaded instances.

interview.q: L4 versus L7 load balancing: when would you choose each?
answer: L4 (TCP/UDP, for example AWS NLB) forwards connections by IP and port without reading them: very high throughput, low latency, static IPs, works for any protocol, can pass TLS through untouched.
L7 (HTTP, for example ALB, nginx, Envoy) reads requests: routing by host, path or header, TLS termination, retries, per-request balancing over multiplexed HTTP/2 connections, WAF integration.
gRPC and HTTP/2 need L7 for per-request balancing; with L4, one long connection pins all requests to one backend.
Common setup: L4 at the edge for scale and static IPs, L7 behind it (ingress or mesh) for HTTP routing.
L7 costs more CPU and adds a hop that has its own timeouts and limits to manage.

interview.q: Design the health checks for a service behind a load balancer in Kubernetes.
answer: Liveness: only “is this process stuck?”. No dependencies, generous thresholds; a failure means restart.
Readiness: “can this pod serve traffic now?”: warm-up finished, not shutting down, local resources fine. A failure removes the pod from the Service but does not restart it.
Startup probe for slow-starting apps, so liveness does not kill them during boot.
Do not make every pod depend on the same shared dependency in a probe; a DB blip should not empty the Service. Prefer degrading (serve cached data, return 503 for affected routes).
Make probes cheap and fast, and align them with the LB's own health checks and the shutdown sequence.

How would you detect a pod that is “alive” but returning 500s?

interview.q: How do you do zero-downtime deploys behind a load balancer, and what can go wrong?
answer: Rolling or blue/green: new instances pass readiness before getting traffic; old ones are drained before stopping.
Shutdown sequence: on SIGTERM fail readiness, wait for the LB to notice, stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close keep-alive sockets, exit within the grace period.
Timeouts lined up: app keep-alive > LB idle timeout, deregistration delay > slowest normal request.
Compatibility: old and new versions run at the same time, so DB migrations and API changes must be backward compatible (expand, then contract).

What goes wrong: 502s from killed connections, long-lived WebSockets dropped at once, cold caches on new instances (use slow start), and a bad version spreading before anyone notices (use canaries and automatic rollback on error rate).
